chapters.n: The book of Alma opens in the first year of the reign of the judges (about 91 BC). Mosiah has died — “gone the way of all the earth” — but his laws remain, accepted by the people and binding on them.

f.w: gone the way of all the earth
f.g: A biblical idiom for dying.

chapters.n: In Alma’s first year as chief judge, a large, notably strong man is brought before him for trial.

f.g: The office of chief judge; Alma is both chief judge and high priest.

chapters.n: This man had been preaching against the church, teaching that religious leaders should seek popularity and be paid by the people rather than work for their own living.

f.g: The opposite of the Nephite church’s practice of unpaid, self-supporting leaders.

chapters.n: His doctrine was attractive: everyone will be saved no matter what, so no one needs to fear, repent, or change. It offered comfort without accountability.

f.w: all mankind should be saved at the last day
f.g: A form of universalism; compare the false teachings warned against in 2 Nephi 28:7-8.

chapters.n: His message became popular enough that many believers began paying him.
Success fed his pride. He began dressing in expensive clothes and founded a church built around his own teachings.

f.g: In the Book of Mormon, expensive clothing often signals pride.

chapters.n: On his way to preach he met a teacher of the church and argued hard, hoping to win church members away. The teacher stood firm, answering with God’s word.

f.w: admonishing him with the words of God

chapters.n: The teacher was Gideon — the same man who years earlier had helped free Limhi’s people from bondage.
Angry at being opposed, the man drew his sword and attacked Gideon. Gideon, now very old, could not defend himself and was killed.

f.g: Very old.

chapters.n: Church members seized the killer and brought him to Alma for judgment.

f.w: to be judged according to the crimes
f.g: He is tried for murder under civil law, not for his beliefs.

chapters.n: He defended himself boldly before Alma.

f.g: Pleaded his case; argued in his own defense.

chapters.n: Alma names the crime: priestcraft, now introduced among the Nephites for the first time — and worse, enforced by the sword. If allowed to spread, it would destroy the nation.

f.g: Preaching for one’s own gain and praise rather than for the welfare of others.

chapters.n: Alma explains that the man had killed a righteous, deeply respected man. To let him go would make the whole people guilty of Gideon’s blood.

f.w: his blood would come upon us

chapters.n: Alma sentences him to death under Mosiah’s law, which the people had accepted. The sentence is for murder, not for teaching false doctrine.

f.w: the law which has been given us by Mosiah

chapters.n: His name was Nehor. Before his execution on the hill Manti, he admitted that his teachings had been contrary to God’s word, and he died a shameful death.

f.g: His “order” of teaching will trouble the Nephites for generations.
Shameful, disgraceful.

chapters.n: Nehor’s death did not stop priestcraft. Many who loved worldly things went on preaching false doctrines for money and honor.

f.w: for the sake of riches and honor

chapters.n: These preachers could not openly lie, for lying was punished, so they claimed to preach their sincere beliefs. Belief itself could not be punished under the law.

f.w: the law could have no power on any man for his belief

f.g: Dared.

chapters.n: Likewise they did not dare steal, rob, or murder — such crimes were punished, and murder by death.
Those outside the church began persecuting those who had taken Christ’s name.

f.w: taken upon them the name of Christ

chapters.n: They mocked and harassed believers for their humility and because members freely shared God’s word without charging money.
The church had a strict rule: members must not persecute non-members, nor one another.
Yet some members grew proud and fought back with their fists — failing the test of persecution in a different way.

f.g: Argue heatedly.

chapters.n: This happened in Alma’s second year as judge and caused the church great trouble.

f.g: A test of faithfulness.

chapters.n: Many hardened their hearts and were removed from church records, and others simply left.
This was hard on the faithful, but they stayed steadfast and immovable, patiently enduring persecution.
A picture of the ideal church: priests and people paused their work to hear God’s word, then all went back to work. Preacher and hearer, teacher and learner, were equals.

f.w: the preacher was no better than the hearer
f.g: The direct opposite of Nehor’s idea that priests should be elevated and supported.

chapters.n: They shared what they had with the poor, needy, sick, and afflicted. They dressed simply but neatly, avoiding showy clothing.

f.g: Clean and attractive, but modest.

chapters.n: By living this way, the church enjoyed continued peace despite persecution.
Because of their steadiness, they became very prosperous, with abundant livestock, grain, precious metals, and fine cloth.

f.g: Young animals fattened for food.
Plain, everyday homemade cloth.

chapters.n: Their prosperity did not make them selfish. They helped anyone in need — old or young, slave or free, member or not — without favoritism. This is how wealth should be used.

f.g: Not playing favorites.
Generous.

chapters.n: They became far wealthier than those outside the church.
Outsiders, by contrast, gave themselves to sorcery, idolatry, idleness, gossip, envy, pride, and many crimes. The law was enforced against lawbreakers as much as possible.

f.g: Empty, foolish talk.
Magic and occult practices.

chapters.n: Consistent enforcement of the law made the wicked quieter, and the Nephites had peace until the fifth year of the judges.
In the fifth year of the judges (about 87 BC), a clever, worldly man named Amlici stirs up conflict. He follows “the order of” Nehor — the same self-serving religion that led to Gideon’s murder.

f.w: after the order of the man that slew Gideon

chapters.n: Amlici gathers a powerful following and tries to have himself made king — exactly the danger Mosiah had warned about.

f.w: establish Amlici to be a king

chapters.n: Church members and other loyal citizens are alarmed, but they know the law: such a change must be decided by the voice of the people.
If Amlici won, he would strip away their religious freedoms, since his real aim was to destroy the church.
People gather throughout the land in groups for and against Amlici, with heated arguments.

f.g: “Wonderful” here means astonishing — remarkably intense disputes.

chapters.n: They cast their votes, and the results are given to the judges.
The people vote against Amlici; he is not made king. The system Mosiah set up works.

f.w: the voice of the people came against Amlici

chapters.n: Amlici’s opponents rejoice, but Amlici stirs his followers to anger.

f.g: Provoke, agitate.

chapters.n: His followers ignore the vote and crown Amlici anyway — rejecting the rule of law.

f.g: Formally set apart or install, here as king.

chapters.n: Amlici immediately orders his people to make war on their own countrymen to force them under his rule.

f.g: Bring them under his control.

chapters.n: His followers become known as Amlicites; the rest are called Nephites, or the people of God.

f.g: Many scholars note similarities with the “Amalekites” of Alma 21-24, possibly the same group under a variant spelling.

chapters.n: The Nephites prepare to defend themselves with every kind of weapon.

f.g: Scimitars — curved swords.

chapters.n: They organize their forces with captains at different levels, ready to meet the attack.

f.g: Senior military commanders.

chapters.n: Amlici arms his people and appoints leaders to wage war against their brethren.

f.g: A civil war — Nephite against Nephite.

chapters.n: The Amlicites attack at the hill Amnihu, east of the river Sidon near Zarahemla.

f.g: The major river of Nephite lands, flowing past Zarahemla.

chapters.n: As chief judge and governor, Alma personally leads the Nephite army into battle.

f.w: the chief judge and the governor

chapters.n: The battle is fierce; the Amlicites fight hard and many Nephites fall.

f.g: The hill Amnihu (verse 15).

chapters.n: But the Lord strengthens the Nephites, and the Amlicites begin to flee.

f.w: the Lord did strengthen the hand of the Nephites

chapters.n: The Nephites pursue all day. The death toll is staggering: 12,532 Amlicites and 6,562 Nephites — the price of one man’s ambition.

f.w: twelve thousand five hundred thirty and two
f.g: Mormon’s precise counts suggest records kept by Nephite officials.

chapters.n: Alma’s army camps for the night in the valley of Gideon, named for the faithful man Nehor killed.
Alma sends spies to follow the retreating Amlicites and learn their plans.

f.g: Scouts sent for military intelligence.

chapters.n: The scouts are named: Zeram, Amnor, Manti, and Limher.

f.g: A name also given to a hill and a land in Nephite territory.

chapters.n: The next day they rush back in alarm.

f.g: Their news is about to explain why.

chapters.n: In the land of Minon, toward the land of Nephi, they saw a huge Lamanite army — and the Amlicites had joined it.

f.g: Mentioned only here; it lay upriver (south) from Zarahemla, toward the land of Nephi.

chapters.n: The combined army was attacking Nephite settlers there, who fled toward Zarahemla. Unless the Nephite army hurried, the capital and their families would fall.

f.w: our fathers, and our wives, and our children

chapters.n: The Nephites break camp and head back toward Zarahemla.
As they cross the river Sidon, the vast Lamanite and Amlicite forces attack them.

f.w: as the sands of the sea
f.g: A common biblical image for a countless multitude.

chapters.n: The Nephites pray mightily for deliverance, and the Lord hears and strengthens them; their enemies begin to fall.
Alma and Amlici meet face to face and fight with swords.

f.g: Single combat between leaders — compare David and Goliath.

chapters.n: Mid-fight, Alma prays — not for glory, but for his life to be spared so he can keep serving and protecting his people.
Strengthened by the Lord, Alma kills Amlici.
Alma then confronts the Lamanite king, who retreats and sends his guards instead.

f.w: the king of the Lamanites fled
f.g: Unlike Alma, the Lamanite king will not risk himself in combat.

chapters.n: Alma and his guards fight the king’s guards until they kill or drive them back.

f.g: Alma’s personal bodyguards.

chapters.n: Alma clears the west bank of the river, throwing the dead into the water so his army has room to cross and fight.
Once the Nephites cross, the enemy — despite overwhelming numbers — breaks and runs.

f.g: Too many to count; the victory is credited to the Lord, not to numbers.

chapters.n: The enemy flees west and north into the wilderness beyond Nephite borders, with the Nephites in pursuit.

f.g: Away from Zarahemla and toward wild, unsettled territory.

chapters.n: Pursued from every side, they scatter into the wilderness of Hermounts, a region full of wild beasts.

f.g: A wilderness mentioned only here, known for dangerous animals.

chapters.n: Many die of their wounds in the wilderness and are eaten by animals and vultures. Their bones were later found and piled up — a grim memorial to the cost of rebellion.

f.g: Mormon, writing centuries later, may be drawing on the original record’s words.

chapters.n: After burying the dead — so many that no one counted them — the surviving Nephites return home to their families.

f.w: the number of the slain were not numbered

chapters.n: The war’s cost reached far beyond soldiers: women and children were killed, livestock lost, and crops trampled by marching armies.

f.g: Trampled.

chapters.n: The enemy dead thrown into the river Sidon were carried away; Mormon says their bones lie in the depths of the sea.

f.w: cast into the waters of Sidon

chapters.n: Mormon pauses the war story to explain a detail: the Amlicites had painted red marks on their foreheads to identify with the Lamanites, though they did not shave their heads as Lamanite warriors did.

f.w: marked themselves with red in their foreheads
f.g: A self-chosen sign of allegiance, like war paint.

chapters.n: Lamanite warriors of this time shaved their heads and wore only loincloths of skin, along with their armor and weapons.

f.g: Shaved or cut short.
Wrapped around the waist.

chapters.n: Mormon recounts the record’s explanation of the Lamanite “mark,” tying it to Laman and Lemuel’s rebellion against Nephi, Jacob, Joseph, and Sam. The Church today rejects any idea that skin color reflects God’s favor; the Book of Mormon itself teaches that all are alike unto God.

f.w: the mark which was set upon their fathers
Nephi, Jacob, and Joseph, and Sam

f.g: In the Book of Mormon the core “curse” is being cut off from the Lord’s presence (2 Nephi 5:20); it is lifted by repentance.

chapters.n: Because Laman, Lemuel, Ishmael’s sons, and their wives tried to kill their brothers, the Lord set a mark upon them, according to the Nephite record.

f.w: their brethren sought to destroy them

chapters.n: The stated purpose of the mark was separation — to keep the Nephites from adopting traditions that would lead them away from God. The concern in the text is belief and covenant, not ancestry.
Those who joined their lives with the Lamanites shared in their separation from the Nephite covenant community.

f.g: Intermarry; the issue throughout is allegiance and belief, as verse 11 makes clear.

chapters.n: Whoever chose to follow the Lamanites was counted as a Lamanite and shared their mark.

f.g: Classified under that name or group.

chapters.n: Mormon defines “Nephite” by faith rather than bloodline: anyone who believed the records from Jerusalem and kept God’s commandments was called a Nephite.

f.w: those records which were brought out of the land of Jerusalem

chapters.n: These faithful Nephites kept the true records of both peoples — the records Mormon is abridging.
Back to the Amlicites: they put a mark on themselves — red paint on their foreheads — by their own choice.

f.w: they set the mark upon themselves
f.g: Mormon’s point: their “mark” was self-inflicted, reflecting their own choice.

chapters.n: Mormon cites a promise to Nephi: the Lamanites would be marked and separated unless they repented and turned to God for mercy. The door to mercy was always open.

f.w: except they repent of their wickedness and turn to me

chapters.n: He quotes another part of the promise: those who joined the Lamanites would share the same mark.

f.w: I will set a mark upon him
f.g: This saying is not preserved in Nephi’s small plates; Mormon may be quoting the large plates.

chapters.n: And: whoever fights against Nephi’s people would bear a mark.
Those who leave the Nephite faith lose the name of Nephi’s seed, while those who are counted as his seed receive the Lord’s blessing — again a matter of choice and covenant.

f.w: he that departeth from thee shall no more be called thy seed

chapters.n: The Amlicites didn’t realize they were fulfilling prophecy when they marked their foreheads. Having openly rebelled against God, they brought the consequences on themselves.
Mormon’s lesson: people bring curses and condemnation upon themselves by their own choices. God does not arbitrarily condemn anyone.

f.w: bring upon himself his own condemnation

chapters.n: Soon after the first battle, another Lamanite army invades at the same spot.

f.g: The Nephites have little time to recover.

chapters.n: An army is sent to drive the invaders out.

f.w: drive them out of their land
f.g: Nephite wars in this book are generally defensive.

chapters.n: Alma, wounded in the earlier battle, does not lead this time.
Alma sends a large army that defeats the Lamanites and pushes them out of Nephite borders.

f.w: out of the borders of their land
f.g: Securing the frontier rather than conquering new territory.

chapters.n: The army returns home, and the land enjoys peace for a while.

f.g: Peace in the book of Alma is often short-lived.

chapters.n: All these wars began and ended within the fifth year of the judges — a single terrible year.

f.g: About 87 BC.

chapters.n: Mormon reflects soberly: in one year tens of thousands entered the next life to receive the reward of the spirit they chose to follow — good or evil.

f.g: The spirit world after death.
Chose, wished.

chapters.n: Each person receives “wages” from whomever he chooses to obey. Our choices determine our master and our reward. So ends the fifth year.

f.w: every man receiveth wages of him whom he listeth to obey

chapters.n: In the sixth year of the judges (about 86 BC), the land of Zarahemla is finally free from war and quarreling.

f.g: Years in Alma are counted from the start of the reign of the judges, about 91 BC.

chapters.n: Yet the people are still grieving: loved ones lost, livestock gone, and fields destroyed by the invaders.
Their suffering humbled them. They saw it as God’s judgment for their sins, and it woke them up to their duty. Hard times can open hearts.

f.w: awakened to a remembrance of their duty

chapters.n: The church grows stronger, and many are baptized in the river Sidon by Alma, whom his father had consecrated as high priest.

f.w: baptized in the waters of Sidon

chapters.n: In the seventh year about 3,500 people join the church, and peace continues.

f.g: A large growth that reflects the humbling of the previous year.

chapters.n: Then comes the familiar turn: in the eighth year, wealth earned by hard work leads church members to pride, seen in their expensive clothing.

f.g: Grow proud.

chapters.n: This deeply troubles Alma and the teachers, priests, and elders he had appointed.

f.g: An office in the Nephite church alongside priests and teachers.

chapters.n: They watch with sorrow as members set their hearts on riches, scorn one another, and persecute non-believers — the reverse of the church’s own rule.

f.w: persecute those that did not believe

chapters.n: Envy, strife, malice, and pride grow in the church until its members are prouder than those outside it.
The church’s wickedness becomes a stumbling block to outsiders, and the church stops growing. A poor example blocks others from the gospel.

f.g: An obstacle that causes others to trip or fall away.

chapters.n: At the start of the ninth year, Alma sees that the church’s example is leading unbelievers deeper into sin, threatening the whole nation.

f.w: from one piece of iniquity to another
f.g: Step by step, small sins lead to larger ones.

chapters.n: He sees great inequality: the proud despising others and ignoring the hungry, thirsty, naked, sick, and afflicted.

f.w: turning their backs upon the needy

chapters.n: In contrast, the humble members were helping the needy, sharing their goods, and enduring hardship for Christ’s sake — the Christ who would come, as prophets had foretold.

f.g: Helping, giving relief to.

f.w: for Christ's sake, who should come

chapters.n: These faithful members looked forward to Christ, kept a remission of their sins, and rejoiced in the coming resurrection through Jesus Christ.

f.w: retaining a remission of their sins
f.g: Staying clean through ongoing faith, service, and humility.

chapters.n: Seeing the faithful persecuted and the inequality, Alma grieves — yet the Spirit of the Lord does not leave him.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord did not fail him
f.g: A comfort for leaders who feel overwhelmed.

chapters.n: Alma chooses a wise elder of the church and, with the people’s approval, gives him the authority to make and enforce laws.

f.w: according to the voice of the people

chapters.n: This man, Nephihah, becomes the new chief judge.
Alma gives up the judgment seat but keeps the office of high priest over the church.

f.w: he retained the office of high priest

chapters.n: His reason: to go among the people and preach, seeing no way to reclaim them except by “bearing down in pure testimony.” He chose the word of God over political power.

f.g: Deceitful cleverness.

chapters.n: So in the ninth year Alma devotes himself fully to the high priesthood and to testifying by the spirit of revelation and prophecy. His great sermons follow.
Free of political duties, Alma begins preaching, starting in Zarahemla and then going throughout the land.
What follows is Alma’s sermon to the church in Zarahemla, taken from his own record. It is one of the most searching sermons in scripture.

f.g: Mormon quotes Alma’s personal writings directly.

chapters.n: Alma establishes his authority — ordained by his father, who held authority from God — and recalls how the church began in the land of Mormon.
He reminds them that God mercifully freed the first believers from King Noah.

f.w: delivered out of the hands of the people of king Noah

chapters.n: Later God freed them again from Lamanite bondage “by the power of his word,” bringing them to Zarahemla, where the church spread.

f.w: by the power of his word

chapters.n: Alma’s first question: have you truly remembered your fathers’ captivity, God’s mercy to them, and how he saved their souls from hell? Remembering is the foundation.
God changed their hearts, waking them from spiritual sleep. In darkness, his word lit their souls when they were bound by death and hell.

f.w: awakened them out of a deep sleep

chapters.n: Were they destroyed? No — a rhetorical question to stir the congregation.

f.g: Alma uses a rapid series of questions — around fifty in this sermon — to prompt self-examination.

chapters.n: Their chains were broken; their souls expanded, and they sang of redeeming love. They are saved.
Now Alma asks: on what conditions were they saved? What gave them hope?
The answer starts with his father’s faith in Abinadi’s words — a holy prophet speaking God’s word.

f.w: the words which were delivered by the mouth of Abinadi

chapters.n: Because of his father’s faith, a mighty change happened in his heart.
His father preached, and their fathers too experienced that change, humbled themselves, trusted God, and stayed faithful to the end. That is how they were saved.
Now the heart of the sermon: have you been spiritually born of God? Does his image show in your face? Have you felt this mighty change? Alma turns history into a personal question.

f.g: Countenance = face or appearance; a changed heart shows outwardly.

chapters.n: Do you have faith in your Creator’s redemption? Can you see yourself, with an eye of faith, resurrected and standing before God to be judged?
Can you imagine hearing the Lord say, “Come unto me, ye blessed,” because your works were righteous?
Or do you imagine you could lie to the Lord on that day about your works and still be saved?

f.g: Nothing is hidden at the judgment.

chapters.n: Or can you picture standing before God full of guilt, with a perfect memory of every wrong and every defiance of his commandments?

f.g: Court of judgment.

chapters.n: Will you be able to look up to God with a pure heart and clean hands, God’s image engraved on your face?

f.w: a pure heart and clean hands

chapters.n: Can you expect salvation after giving yourself over to the devil’s rule?
No one can be saved unless his garments are washed white through the blood of the coming Redeemer. Salvation is through Christ’s Atonement.
Imagine standing at God’s judgment bar with garments stained with blood and filth — what would they testify about you?

f.g: The judgment seat of God.

chapters.n: Those stains would testify of murder and every kind of sin.

f.g: Possibly literal for some; also, ancient prophets spoke of being guilty of others’ blood when failing them.

chapters.n: Could such a person sit down in God’s kingdom with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the holy prophets, whose garments are spotless?

f.w: with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob

chapters.n: No — unless God is a liar. The unrepentant will be cast out as children of the devil’s kingdom.

f.g: God’s word that no unclean thing can enter his kingdom cannot fail.

chapters.n: One of scripture’s most quoted questions: if you once felt to sing the song of redeeming love, can you feel so now? Conversion must be kept alive.

f.g: Past spiritual experience is not enough; Alma asks about today.

chapters.n: If you were to die right now, could you say you have been humble enough, with garments cleansed by Christ’s blood?

f.w: if ye were called to die at this time

chapters.n: Are you stripped of pride? If not, you are not prepared to meet God. Prepare quickly.

f.g: An image of removing filthy clothing — a pointed contrast to the church’s costly apparel.

chapters.n: Are you stripped of envy? Envy, too, leaves a person unprepared — and no one knows when the hour will come.

f.w: he knoweth not when the time shall come

chapters.n: Does anyone mock or persecute his brother?

f.w: make a mock of his brother

chapters.n: Woe to that person; he is not prepared and must repent or he cannot be saved.

f.g: An expression of grief and warning — “alas for.”

chapters.n: Alma calls all workers of iniquity to repent, for the Lord has spoken.
But the message is full of hope: God invites everyone, with arms of mercy stretched out, saying “Repent, and I will receive you.”

f.w: the arms of mercy are extended

chapters.n: Come unto him and partake of the fruit of the tree of life, freely eating and drinking the bread and waters of life.

f.w: the fruit of the tree of life
bread and the waters of life

chapters.n: Come and bring forth works of righteousness, and you will not be cut down and burned like a fruitless tree.

f.w: hewn down and cast into the fire

chapters.n: Those who bear no good fruit will soon have reason to mourn.
Alma addresses those who claimed to know righteousness but wandered off like sheep without a shepherd — though the Shepherd keeps calling.

f.g: Swollen with pride.

chapters.n: The Good Shepherd calls you by his own name — the name of Christ, which you took upon you. If you won’t hear him, you are not his sheep.
If not his sheep, whose are you? Alma bluntly says the devil is the shepherd of those who reject Christ.

f.g: A fold is a sheep pen; Alma forces a choice between two flocks.

chapters.n: All good comes from God, and all evil from the devil — a simple test for discerning.

f.w: whatsoever is good cometh from God

chapters.n: Your works show whose voice you are following: good works follow the Good Shepherd; evil works follow the devil.
Those who follow the devil receive his “wages” — spiritual death, cut off from all good works.
Alma speaks with all the energy of his soul, plainly, so no one can misunderstand.

f.g: With all his strength and intensity.

chapters.n: He is called to speak this way by the holy order of God, testifying of what the prophets foretold.
And beyond his calling, Alma knows these things for himself. How does he know?
He fasted and prayed for many days, and the Holy Spirit revealed the truth to him. His testimony came by the same means available to anyone who seeks.

f.w: I have fasted and prayed many days

chapters.n: The Spirit also confirmed that the words of earlier prophets are true.
Alma’s witness: Jesus Christ, the Only Begotten Son, full of grace, mercy, and truth, will come to take away the sins of all who steadfastly believe.

f.w: full of grace, and mercy, and truth
take away the sins of the world

chapters.n: His calling is to preach to everyone — old, middle-aged, and young, bond and free — that they must repent and be born again.
The Spirit declares: repent, all the earth, for the Son of God is coming in glory and power — the King of heaven will soon shine among mankind.

f.w: the kingdom of heaven is soon at hand

chapters.n: The Spirit cries to Alma with a mighty voice: tell this people that without repentance they cannot inherit heaven.
The ax is already at the root of the tree: every fruitless tree will be cut down. Alma echoes John the Baptist, who would preach this a century later.

f.w: the ax is laid at the root of the tree

chapters.n: Alma asks whether they can ignore these warnings and keep trampling the Holy One, chasing pride, costly clothing, and riches.

f.w: trample the Holy One under your feet

chapters.n: Will they keep thinking themselves better than others and persecute the humble members whose lives show real repentance?

f.g: Fitting, worthy of repentance.

chapters.n: Will they keep turning away the poor and withholding their goods? Alma names the exact sins he saw in Alma 4.

f.w: turning your backs upon the poor

chapters.n: Those who persist in wickedness will be cut down unless they quickly repent.
Alma calls the faithful to separate themselves from wickedness. The unrepentant will be removed from church records so the names of the wicked are not mingled with the righteous.

f.w: come ye out from the wicked, and be ye separate
their names shall be blotted out

chapters.n: The righteous will be written in the book of life and receive an inheritance at God’s right hand. Objections cannot change God’s word.
Alma uses an image every herdsman knew: a shepherd guards his sheep and drives out — or kills — any wolf that enters.
The Good Shepherd invites them into his fold and commands them not to let ravenous wolves — false teachers and harmful influences — in among them.
Alma speaks with the Lord’s own authority: obey these words.

f.w: in the language of him who hath commanded me
f.g: Alma speaks as the Lord’s messenger.

chapters.n: To church members he speaks as a command; to others, as an invitation: come, be baptized, and partake of the fruit of the tree of life.

f.w: Come and be baptized unto repentance

chapters.n: After his sermon, Alma ordains priests and elders by the laying on of hands to lead and watch over the church in Zarahemla.
Non-members who repented were baptized and welcomed into the church — Alma’s invitation was accepted.
Members who stayed proud and would not repent were removed from church records, as Alma had warned.
In this way the church in Zarahemla was set in order again.

f.g: Its proper organization and standards.

chapters.n: Mormon stresses that God’s word was freely available to all; no one was barred from attending meetings to hear it.

f.g: Freely given to everyone.

chapters.n: Mormon closes the account of Ammon and his brothers — their journeys, sufferings, and “incomprehensible joy” — and blesses their souls forever.

chapters.n: Alma, the chief missionary of the Nephite church, pours out a heartfelt wish: if only he were an angel, he could preach repentance to everyone on earth at once with a voice no one could ignore.

chapters.n: His motive is love, not fame. He longs for every person to hear about repentance and God’s plan to redeem them, so that the sorrow sin causes would end everywhere.
Alma catches himself. Wishing for a different role than the one God gave him is a kind of discontent. True disciples serve faithfully where they have been placed.

f.g: Assigned or given as one’s portion.

chapters.n: God respects agency. He gives people what they truly desire—life or death, salvation or destruction—and those outcomes follow fixed, fair laws. Alma should not try to stir up or overturn that just arrangement.

f.g: To rake up or disturb, like a harrow breaking up soil.

chapters.n: Everyone eventually meets both good and evil. Those who cannot tell the difference (like little children) are not held guilty, but those who know are judged by what they choose and desire.
Knowing that God handles things justly, Alma asks himself why he should want anything more than to do the work he was actually called to do.
He repeats the question to settle it in his own heart: there is no need to wish for an angel’s trumpet voice.

The same God who freed Israel from Egypt also freed Alma’s own fathers (the people of Alma the Elder) from bondage. Alma sees one consistent, delivering God across history.
That God established His church, called Alma to preach, and blessed his work with success. Alma says this fills his joy completely.
His joy grows even fuller because of his friends, the sons of Mosiah, who spent fourteen years preaching among the Lamanites in the land of Nephi.
Their labor was intense, and thousands of Lamanites were converted. Alma rejoices at the great reward awaiting them.
Thinking of their success, Alma feels so much joy that it is almost as if his spirit could leave his body. It echoes Ammon’s overwhelming joy in Alma 27.
Alma closes with a prayer that his fellow missionaries and all their converts may dwell in God’s kingdom forever, never to leave, praising Him eternally.

Mormon picks up the story after the war of Alma 28. The converted Lamanites, the people of Ammon, are now settled safely in Jershon, and the invading Lamanites have been driven out and the dead buried.
The losses were so great no one counted the dead. After a season of fasting, mourning, and prayer, the sixteenth year of the judges (about 76 BC) brings a long-awaited peace.
The Nephites live the law of Moses faithfully, understanding that it pointed forward to Christ and would be kept only until He fulfilled it.
The entire sixteenth year passes without trouble—a rare and welcome stretch of calm in a war-filled record.
Peace continues into the seventeenth year of the judges.
Late that year a man arrives in Zarahemla preaching against prophecies of Christ. Mormon calls him an “Anti-Christ”: someone who opposes Christ and His saving role.
Nephite law protected freedom of belief. God Himself forbade laws that would treat people unequally because of what they believed.

The principle is summed up: people were judged for crimes they committed, not for beliefs they held. That fairness put everyone “on equal grounds.”

f.g: Equal standing before the law.

Each worshipper climbs up, raises his hands to heaven, and shouts the same words aloud—a public show of religion.
The Zoramite prayer begins. They describe God as a spirit only, now and forever—denying that God has a body or could come to earth as Christ.
They thank God for making them better than others, scorn their brethren’s beliefs as childish, claim to be uniquely chosen, and declare there will be no Christ.

chapters.n: Alma and his companions are stunned beyond words by what they hear.

f.g: A Nephite-era name the text interprets as “the holy stand.”

chapters.n: Mormon summarizes the prayer’s theme: gratitude for being chosen and for not believing in “things to come”—that is, in a future Christ, the same argument Korihor made.
Afterward they go home and never mention God again until the next week. Their religion is a once-a-week ritual with no effect on daily life.

f.w: never speaking of their God again

chapters.n: Alma is grieved. Behind the ritual he sees hearts fixed on gold, silver, and fine goods.

f.g: Proud; puffed up.

chapters.n: Alma begins his own prayer—a striking contrast to the Rameumptom. He asks how long God’s servants must live amid such open wickedness.

f.w: cry unto thee with their mouths

chapters.n: Alma describes their expensive clothes, curled hair, bracelets, and gold. Their hearts are set on these things even as they thank God they alone are chosen.

chapters.n: He asks God to comfort his soul “in Christ”—the very Being the Zoramites deny—and to help him bear patiently the trials ahead.
Alma then prays for each of his companions by name, asking God to comfort them in Christ and give them success.
He asks that they all have strength to endure the trials this mission will bring.
His real goal is clear: to bring the Zoramites back to God through Christ.
The heart of the prayer: these souls are precious, and many are family. Alma asks for power and wisdom to win them back, showing love even for people he has just criticized.
Alma lays his hands on his companions, and they are filled with the Holy Spirit.

f.g: Placed his hands on them, as in a blessing.

chapters.n: The missionaries split up to cover more ground, not worrying about food, drink, or clothing—trusting God as Jesus later taught His disciples.
The Lord answers Alma’s prayer: they do not go hungry or thirsty, and any suffering is swallowed up in the joy of Christ—because Alma prayed in faith.

f.w: swallowed up in the joy of Christ

chapters.n: The missionaries preach everywhere they can: in synagogues, in homes, and even out in the streets.
After much effort, the first people to respond are the poor, who had been thrown out of the synagogues because their clothes were too rough and plain.
Treated like filth and trash by their own people, these Zoramites are poor in possessions—and that hardship has also made them “poor in heart,” meaning humble and teachable.

f.g: Worthless waste skimmed off melted metal.

chapters.n: While Alma teaches on the hill Onidah, a large crowd of these humble poor comes to him.

f.g: A hill in Antionum; mentioned only here.

chapters.n: Their spokesman explains their plight: despised for their poverty, especially by their priests, they’ve been barred from synagogues they built with their own hands. “What shall we do?”
Alma turns to face him with great joy. He sees that their suffering has humbled them and prepared them to receive God’s word.
Alma stops addressing the other crowd and turns to these sincere, penitent listeners.
His first words are a blessing: if you are lowly in heart, you are blessed.
Alma repeats their question back to them to show he heard it.
Do you really think you can worship God only inside a synagogue? Worship is not limited to a building.
And do you think worship happens only once a week? Alma gently contrasts true discipleship with the Zoramites’ weekly ritual.
Alma says being cast out was actually good for them. Rejection and poverty have made them humble, and humility is where wisdom begins.
Being forced into humility can lead a person to repent. Whoever repents finds mercy, and whoever finds mercy and endures to the end will be saved.
But Alma raises the bar: aren’t those who humble themselves because of God’s word even more blessed than those humbled by circumstances?
The person who chooses humility, repents, and endures is far more blessed than one whose humility comes only from hardship.
Most blessed are those who believe God’s word and are baptized without a stubborn heart—who don’t demand absolute proof before they will believe.
Many people say, “Give me a sign from heaven and then I’ll believe”—exactly what Korihor demanded.
Alma explains that this is not faith. Once you know something for certain, you no longer need to believe it.
Knowledge also brings greater accountability. Someone who knows God’s will and disobeys is more condemned than someone who only believes and stumbles.

f.w: knoweth the will of God and doeth it not

chapters.n: Alma invites them to weigh this for themselves: each person is judged by their works, whether they have knowledge or only belief.
Alma’s famous definition: faith is not perfect knowledge. It is hoping for things that are not seen but are true.

f.w: faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things

chapters.n: God is merciful to all who believe in Him, so His first desire is that we simply believe His word.
God speaks His word through angels to men and women alike, and sometimes even through little children whose words amaze the wise and learned.
Alma turns back to their situation and assures them he does not mean to judge them harshly.
He doesn’t assume all of them were forced into humility. He believes some would be humble no matter what their circumstances.
Just as faith is not perfect knowledge, they cannot know at first that Alma’s words are true. Certainty grows over time.
Alma invites them to “experiment” on his words. Even a small particle of faith—even just the desire to believe—is enough to begin, if they let that desire work in them.

He compares God’s word to a seed. If you make room for it and don’t throw it out through unbelief, a good seed will begin to swell inside you. It enlarges your soul, enlightens your mind, and starts to taste delicious.

f.w: compare the word unto a seed

chapters.n: Wouldn’t that growth strengthen your faith? Yes—though it is not yet perfect knowledge.
As the seed sprouts and grows, you can say with confidence that it is good. Visible growth strengthens faith.
Can you be sure the seed is good? Yes, because every seed produces after its own kind. Good growth reveals a good seed.

f.w: every seed bringeth forth unto its own likeness

chapters.n: If a seed grows, it is good; if it doesn’t, it is thrown away. Results are the test.
Since they tried the experiment and the seed is growing, they can know it is good.
On that one point their knowledge is now perfect, and faith about it rests (is “dormant”). They know the word has enlarged their souls and expanded their minds.

f.g: Resting or inactive—no longer needed on that point because it has become knowledge.

chapters.n: Is this real? Yes, because it is light, and light can be seen and recognized as good. Spiritual growth is genuine evidence.
But having tasted this light, is their knowledge complete? No. They have only used faith to plant and test the seed, so they must keep exercising faith.
As the seed becomes a tree, they must nourish it with great care so it can take root, grow, and bear fruit.
If they neglect it, it will never root deeply; when the sun’s heat comes, it will wither and be thrown away—like the seed on stony ground in Jesus’ parable.

f.w: because it hath no root it withers away

chapters.n: The failure is not the seed’s fault or the fruit’s. It is because the soil is barren and the tree was not cared for.

f.g: Unable to produce growth.

chapters.n: Without nourishing the word and looking forward in faith, you can never taste the fruit of the tree of life.
But nourish it diligently and patiently, with faith, and it will take root and become a tree “springing up unto everlasting life.”
In time they will taste its fruit—sweeter, whiter, and purer than anything else—and feast until they never hunger or thirst again. This echoes Lehi’s vision of the tree whose fruit is God’s love.

f.w: sweet above all that is sweet
hunger not, neither shall ye thirst

chapters.n: Then they will receive the reward of their faith, diligence, patience, and long-suffering as they waited for the tree to bear fruit.

f.g: Patient endurance over a long time.

chapters.n: The humble Zoramites have practical questions: Should they believe in one God? How do they plant this seed? Where should they begin exercising faith?
Alma corrects a misunderstanding. They are wrong to think they cannot worship outside the synagogue, and if they read the scriptures that way, they have misunderstood them.
Alma turns to Zenos, an Israelite prophet whose writings were on the brass plates but are not in our Bible.
Alma quotes Zenos’s prayer. God heard him even in the wilderness, and when he prayed about his enemies, God softened them toward him.
God also heard Zenos praying out in his field—prayer works wherever you are working.
When Zenos went home, God heard him there too.
And in his “closet”—a private inner room—God heard his secret prayers.

f.g: A small private room, not a clothes cupboard.

chapters.n: God is merciful to His children who pray to be heard by Him rather than to impress people—a quiet rebuke of the Rameumptom.

f.w: to be heard of thee and not of men

chapters.n: God heard Zenos in congregations, too. Public worship has its place when hearts are sincere.
Most relevant to Alma’s listeners: God heard Zenos when he was cast out and despised by his enemies, and He dealt with those enemies.
Zenos explains why God heard him: because of his afflictions, his sincerity, and above all “because of thy Son.” God’s mercy flows through Jesus Christ.
Alma asks: do you believe the ancient scriptures?
If you do, then you must accept what Zenos said—that God turns away judgment because of His Son.
If they have truly read the scriptures, how can they deny the Son of God? The Zoramites claimed scripture but rejected its central figure.
Zenos was not alone. Another ancient prophet, Zenock, said the same things.
Zenock taught that God is displeased with people who refuse to understand the mercies He offers through His Son.
Zenock was stoned to death for this testimony—a reminder that witnesses of Christ have often suffered for it.
Alma adds that many other prophets also testified of the Son of God.

Moses spoke of Him too. In the wilderness Moses raised a bronze serpent on a pole, and anyone bitten by poisonous snakes could look at it and live. It was a “type,” or symbol, of Christ lifted up on the cross.

f.w: a type was raised up in the wilderness

f.g: A person, object, or event that foreshadows Christ.

chapters.n: Few understood what the serpent meant. Some were so hard-hearted they refused to look and died—because they did not believe something so simple could heal them.

f.w: they did not believe that it would heal them

chapters.n: Alma asks them directly: if you could be healed just by looking, wouldn’t you look right away? Or would you be too stubborn or lazy and perish?

f.g: Lazy.

chapters.n: So “look” and believe in the Son of God: that He will come, suffer and die for sins, rise again to bring the resurrection, and judge all people by their works. This is the seed Alma wants them to plant.

f.w: begin to believe in the Son of God

chapters.n: Alma brings his seed comparison full circle: plant this word about Christ in your hearts and nourish it, and it will grow into a tree of everlasting life. Through Christ’s joy their burdens can be made light—and they can do this if they choose.

f.w: plant this word in your hearts

chapters.n: Alma sits down, and his longtime companion Amulek rises to add a second witness to what Alma has taught.
Amulek points out that these Zoramites must have been taught plenty about Christ before they broke away from the Nephites.

f.g: Breaking away in disagreement.

chapters.n: He reminds them they had asked Alma what to do in their afflictions, and that Alma prepared their minds by urging faith and patience.
Alma had asked them to have enough faith to plant the word and test its goodness.
Amulek names their real question: is salvation found in the Son of God, or is there no Christ at all, as their leaders taught?

f.w: whether the word be in the Son of God

chapters.n: He affirms that Alma has shown, in many ways, that salvation comes through Christ.
Alma’s evidence included Zenos, Zenock, and Moses.
Now Amulek adds his own testimony: he knows Christ will come, take on His people’s transgressions, and atone for the sins of the world.

f.g: To reconcile; to make “at one” by paying sin’s price.

chapters.n: An atonement is necessary. Under God’s plan, without it all humanity would inevitably perish, because everyone is fallen and lost.

f.w: all are fallen and are lost

f.g: Necessary; required.

chapters.n: This must be “a great and last sacrifice”—not of a human, animal, or bird, but infinite and eternal. Christ’s sacrifice ends the need for all the animal sacrifices that pointed to it.
No mere man can pay for another’s sins with his own blood. Even a just human court would not execute an innocent brother in place of a murderer.
The law demands the guilty party’s life, so only an infinite atonement—one beyond any human capacity—can cover the sins of the whole world.
With this final sacrifice, the shedding of blood in sacrifices would stop and the law of Moses would be completely fulfilled, down to its smallest detail.

f.g: The smallest letter and mark in Hebrew writing—every tiny detail.

f.w: a stop to the shedding of blood

chapters.n: This is the whole point of the law of Moses: every part of it pointed to the great and last sacrifice of the Son of God.

f.w: every whit pointing to that great and last sacrifice

f.g: The smallest part.

chapters.n: Christ brings salvation to those who believe. His sacrifice opens the way for mercy to overpower justice and makes it possible for people to have “faith unto repentance.”

f.g: Deep, tender compassion; the bowels were thought of as the seat of feelings.

chapters.n: Mercy satisfies justice’s demands and wraps the repentant in safety. But anyone who does not exercise faith unto repentance remains exposed to the full demands of justice.

f.w: mercy can satisfy the demands of justice

chapters.n: Amulek prays that they will begin to exercise faith unto repentance and call on God’s name for mercy.
Cry to Him for mercy, for He is mighty to save.

Here begins Amulek’s great list of places and reasons to pray—an answer to the Zoramites’ belief that worship happens only on the Rameumptom. Pray in your fields and over your flocks.
Pray at home for your whole household, morning, midday, and evening.
Pray for protection from your enemies.
Pray against the devil, the enemy of everything good.

f.w: the devil, who is an enemy to all righteousness

chapters.n: Pray over your crops so they will prosper—God cares about ordinary daily needs.
Pray over your flocks so they will grow.
Pour out your souls in private places, too—in closets, secret places, and the wilderness.
Even when you are not praying aloud, keep your heart full and drawn out toward God continually, for yourself and for those around you.

f.w: drawn out in prayer unto him continually

chapters.n: But prayer alone is not enough. If you turn away the needy, the naked, the sick, and the afflicted, and won’t share what you have, your prayers are empty and you are a hypocrite.

f.g: Share your possessions.

chapters.n: Without charity, a person is like dross—worthless waste that refiners throw out to be walked on.

f.g: Impurities skimmed off molten metal and discarded.

chapters.n: Having received so many witnesses from scripture, they should now bring forth the fruits of repentance—real change in how they live.
Don’t harden your hearts any longer. Now is the time of salvation, and if you repent, the plan of redemption will take effect for you immediately.

f.w: now is the time and the day of your salvation

chapters.n: One of the Book of Mormon’s best-known teachings: this life is the time to prepare to meet God and to do the work that prepares us for eternity.

f.w: this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God

chapters.n: Don’t put off repenting until the end. If we don’t use our time well in this life, a “night of darkness” follows when that work can no longer be done in the same way.

f.g: To delay or put off.

f.w: night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed

chapters.n: You can’t count on a deathbed change of heart. The same spirit—the same desires and character—you have when you leave this life will remain with you in the next.
Someone who delays repentance until death becomes subject to the devil, who “seals” them as his. The Lord’s Spirit withdraws, and that is the final state of the wicked.
Amulek knows this because the Lord does not dwell in unholy temples, but in righteous hearts. The righteous will dwell in His kingdom forever, their garments made white through the Lamb’s blood.

f.w: he dwelleth not in unholy temples
made white through the blood of the Lamb

chapters.n: Remember these things. Work out your salvation with reverence before God, and stop denying that Christ will come.

f.w: work out your salvation with fear

chapters.n: Stop resisting the Holy Ghost, take Christ’s name upon you, humble yourselves, worship God wherever you are “in spirit and in truth,” and live every day with gratitude for His blessings.
Stay alert through constant prayer so the devil cannot overpower you and claim you at the last day, for he gives nothing good in return.
Be patient in trials. Don’t lash out at those who threw you out for being poor, or you will become sinners just like them.

f.g: To insult or speak abusively against.

chapters.n: Bear your afflictions patiently, with a firm hope that someday you will rest from them all.
After Amulek’s sermon, Alma and Amulek leave the crowd and travel to Jershon, home of the people of Ammon.
The other missionaries finish preaching among the Zoramites and join them in Jershon.
The Zoramite elite meet to discuss the missionaries’ message and grow angry, because it threatens their “craft”—the system of priestcraft and wealth that kept them in power.

f.g: Trade or scheme; here, the power and income their false religion gave them.

chapters.n: They gather people from all over the land to find out what everyone thinks of the preaching.
The rulers, priests, and teachers hide their real intentions and quietly find out where each person stands.

f.g: Secretly; privately.

chapters.n: Everyone who sides with Alma’s message is expelled. Many believers are driven out and flee to Jershon.
Alma and his brethren care for these refugees.

f.g: To serve and care for.

chapters.n: The wicked chief ruler of the Zoramites demands that the people of Ammon expel the refugees from Jershon.
Despite threats, the people of Ammon are not afraid. They welcome the poor Zoramites, feeding and clothing them, giving them land, and meeting their needs—the very charity Amulek had just preached.

f.w: did nourish them, and did clothe them

chapters.n: This kindness enrages the Zoramites, who begin mingling with the Lamanites and stirring them up against the people of Ammon.
The Zoramites and Lamanites start preparing for war against both the people of Ammon and the Nephites.
So ends the seventeenth year of the reign of the judges (about 75 BC).
The peaceful people of Ammon, who had covenanted never to fight, move to Melek so Nephite armies can occupy Jershon. War begins in the eighteenth year; Mormon promises to describe it later.

f.w: an account shall be given of their wars hereafter

chapters.n: Alma, Ammon, the others, and Alma’s two sons return to Zarahemla after helping many Zoramites repent. Those converts now live in Jershon and are prepared to defend their families and lands.

f.w: instruments in the hands of God

chapters.n: Alma is grieved by the wars and contention, and especially that people are growing hard-hearted and offended by the “strictness of the word”—teachings that call for real change.

f.g: Grow hard.

chapters.n: So Alma gathers his sons and gives each one a personal charge about righteousness. Mormon includes these talks from Alma’s own record in chapters 36–42.

f.g: Instructions or responsibility given to someone.

chapters.n: Alma begins his counsel to his eldest son, Helaman, with a promise repeated throughout the Book of Mormon: keep God’s commandments and you will prosper in the land. Many readers notice this chapter is arranged as a large chiasm, with Christ at its center (verses 17–18).

f.w: ye shall prosper in the land

chapters.n: Alma urges Helaman to remember, as he has, how the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob delivered their ancestors from bondage. Only God could free them.

f.w: remembering the captivity of our fathers

chapters.n: Since Helaman is young, Alma pleads with him to learn from his father. Anyone who trusts God will be supported through trials and lifted up at the last day.
Alma clarifies that his knowledge did not come from himself or from worldly thinking, but from God.

f.g: Ordinary, worldly human thinking.

chapters.n: Without being “born of God” he would not know these things. God made them known to him through an angel—not because Alma deserved it.
Alma recounts that he and the sons of Mosiah were actively trying to destroy the church when God sent an angel to stop them.

f.w: seeking to destroy the church of God

chapters.n: The angel’s voice was like thunder; the earth shook, and they all fell to the ground in fear.
The voice told Alma to stand up, and he rose and saw the angel.
The angel’s warning: unless you want to be destroyed yourself, stop trying to destroy God’s church.

f.w: If thou wilt of thyself be destroyed

chapters.n: Alma collapsed and for three days and nights could not speak or move.
The angel said more, which his companions heard, but Alma heard nothing after that warning because he was overwhelmed by fear that he would be destroyed.
Alma describes his soul as “racked” and “harrowed up”—tortured and torn—by the memory of every sin he had committed.

f.g: Tortured, as if stretched on a rack.
Torn and churned, as soil is by a harrow.

chapters.n: He remembered every sin and felt the pains of hell, seeing clearly that he had rebelled against God.
He had spiritually “murdered” many by leading them away from God. The thought of standing before God filled him with unspeakable horror.
He wished he could simply cease to exist, body and soul, rather than face God’s judgment.
For three days and nights he felt the pain of a damned soul—completely cut off from hope.
The turning point. In his torment, Alma remembered his father, Alma the Elder, prophesying of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who would atone for the world’s sins.

f.w: I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy

chapters.n: His mind “caught hold” of that thought, and he cried out in his heart: “O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me.” This short prayer is the center of Alma’s story and of the chapter.

f.w: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me

f.g: Extreme bitterness, like bile.

chapters.n: As soon as he prayed, the pain was gone, and the memory of his sins no longer tormented him.

f.w: I could remember my pains no more

chapters.n: In its place came overwhelming joy and marvelous light—joy as intense as his pain had been.
Nothing could be as sharp and bitter as his pain, and nothing as sharp and sweet as his joy. The words mirror each other, matching the chapter’s balanced structure.

f.g: Intensely felt—extremely sharp or keen.

chapters.n: Alma saw a vision like Lehi’s: God on His throne surrounded by countless angels singing praises, and he longed to be there. Verse 22 repeats 1 Nephi 1:8 almost word for word.

f.w: even as our father Lehi saw

f.g: Crowds or assemblies.

chapters.n: His strength returned, and he stood up and testified that he had been born of God.
Ever since, he has worked tirelessly to help others repent and taste the same joy—to be born of God and filled with the Holy Ghost.
The Lord gives Alma great joy in the results of his missionary work.
Many others have been born of God and seen what he has seen. Their knowledge, like his, comes from God.
God has supported Alma through every kind of trial, delivering him from prison, bonds, and death. He trusts God will keep delivering him.
He knows God will raise him up to dwell in glory. He praises God for bringing Israel out of Egypt, drowning the Egyptians in the Red Sea, and leading them to the promised land.

f.w: swallowed up the Egyptians in the Red Sea

chapters.n: God also brought Lehi’s family out of Jerusalem and has delivered them many times since. Alma always remembers these deliverances and urges Helaman to do the same.

f.w: brought our fathers out of the land of Jerusalem

chapters.n: Alma closes as he opened: keeping the commandments brings prosperity, but refusing to keep them cuts a person off from God’s presence. The opening and closing promises frame the whole chapter.
Alma now hands Helaman the sacred records he has been guarding. Helaman becomes the next keeper of the Nephite scriptures and history.
Helaman must continue writing the people’s history on the plates of Nephi and keep everything sacred, as Alma did, because these records serve a wise purpose.
The brass plates, brought from Jerusalem by Nephi, contain the holy scriptures and the genealogy of their ancestors back to the beginning.
Prophets foretold that these plates would be preserved by the Lord and passed down until they reached every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.
If cared for, the plates will keep their brightness—metal records that do not tarnish, along with all plates containing scripture.

f.g: Sacred scripture.

chapters.n: A key principle: God brings about great things through small and simple means. Something as modest as metal plates can change countless lives.

f.w: by small and simple things are great things brought to pass

f.g: To confuse or overturn.

chapters.n: God works through ordinary “means” to accomplish His eternal purposes, using small things to humble the wise and save many souls.
The records have enlarged the people’s memory, convinced many of their errors, and led them to know God and be saved.
Without these records, Ammon and his brothers could not have converted thousands of Lamanites. The scriptures led them to know God and rejoice in Christ their Redeemer.
Alma hopes the records will bring many more thousands—Lamanites and stubborn Nephites alike—to know their Redeemer. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the Book of Mormon today.

f.g: Stubborn; refusing to bend or obey.

chapters.n: Alma admits he doesn’t fully understand all the purposes of these records yet, so he won’t speculate.

f.g: Hold back; refrain.

chapters.n: It is enough to know God has a wise purpose. His paths are straight and His course is “one eternal round”—consistent and unchanging.
Alma pleads with Helaman to remember how exact God’s commandments are, and repeats the core promise: obedience brings prosperity, and disobedience cuts one off from God.
God has entrusted Helaman with sacred things that He will preserve to show His power to future generations.
Alma warns prophetically: if Helaman disobeys, the sacred records will be taken from him and he will be left to Satan, who will scatter him like chaff in the wind.

f.g: Husks blown away when grain is threshed.

chapters.n: But if he obeys and seeks the Lord’s direction for how to use the records, no earthly or hellish power can take them from him.

f.w: no power of earth or hell

chapters.n: God will keep every promise He makes to Helaman, just as He kept His promises to their fathers.
God promised to preserve these records to display His power to future generations.
One purpose is already fulfilled: thousands of Lamanites restored to the truth. More will follow in future generations.
So Alma commands Helaman to be diligent in following his counsel and keeping the written commandments.

Alma turns to the twenty-four gold plates found by Limhi’s people—the Jaredite record. Helaman should keep them so the wickedness of that destroyed nation can be made known, and also preserve the “interpreters” used to translate them.
The Jaredites began doing evil in secret—murders and abominations—and the Lord warned that unless they repented they would be destroyed.

f.g: A name given to the servant who would use the stone; its exact meaning is uncertain.

chapters.n: These interpreters were prepared so that God’s word would be fulfilled.
God’s word: He will bring secret works and abominations from darkness to light, destroy the unrepentant, and reveal their secrets to every later nation in the land.

f.w: bring forth out of darkness unto light

chapters.n: The Jaredites did not repent, so they were destroyed, and their secret evils have now been revealed to the Nephites—just as God said.
Helaman must withhold the actual oaths, covenants, signs, and secret methods of their conspiracies so that the people don’t imitate them and fall into the same darkness.

f.g: Keep back; withhold.

chapters.n: A curse rests on this land: those who work in darkness will be destroyed when they are “fully ripe” in wickedness. Alma doesn’t want his people to meet that fate.
Helaman should share the Jaredites’ crimes and their outcome, teaching people to hate such evil and recognize it as the cause of destruction—without teaching them how it was done.

f.g: To hate deeply.

chapters.n: The Jaredites killed the prophets sent to warn them. Their victims’ blood cried to God for justice, and judgment came upon these secret combinations.

f.w: the blood of those whom they murdered did cry

f.g: Secret conspiracies bound by oaths to gain power or wealth through crime.

chapters.n: Alma repeats the curse: those who work in darkness and secret combinations will be destroyed unless they repent before they are fully ripe.
Don’t reveal the secret plans; instead, teach the people an everlasting hatred of sin.
Preach repentance and faith in Jesus Christ. Teach humility and meekness, and teach people to resist every temptation through faith in Christ.
Teach them never to tire of doing good and to stay meek and humble, for such people find rest for their souls.

f.w: never be weary of good works

chapters.n: A father’s plea to a young son: learn wisdom while you are young—learn to keep God’s commandments now.
Look to God for every kind of support. Let all you do, everywhere you go, every thought, and every affection of your heart be centered on the Lord.

f.w: let all thy thoughts be directed unto the Lord

chapters.n: Counsel with the Lord in everything, and He will guide you for good. Pray at night for His watchcare and wake with a grateful heart; then you will be lifted up at the last day.

f.w: Counsel with the Lord in all thy doings

chapters.n: Don’t be lazy because the way is easy. Like the Israelites who only had to look at the bronze serpent to live, we only need to look to Christ and live forever.

f.w: if they would look they might live

chapters.n: Alma’s farewell charge to Helaman: take care of these sacred things, look to God and live, preach to the people, and be serious-minded. Then a simple, tender goodbye.

f.g: Serious, thoughtful, self-controlled.

chapters.n: Alma now speaks to his second son, Shiblon, opening with the same promise he gave Helaman: keep the commandments and prosper; disobey and be cut off from God.

f.w: even as I said unto Helaman

chapters.n: Alma expects great joy in Shiblon because of his steadiness and faithfulness. Having started young, he hopes Shiblon will continue, since those who endure to the end are blessed.

f.w: blessed is he that endureth to the end

chapters.n: Shiblon has already given his father joy through his faithfulness, diligence, patience, and endurance on the Zoramite mission.
Alma knows Shiblon was imprisoned and stoned for preaching, yet bore it patiently because the Lord was with him and delivered him.

f.g: In chains or imprisoned.

chapters.n: The more Shiblon trusts God, the more God will deliver him from trials and lift him up at the last day.
Alma again explains that his knowledge comes from God’s Spirit, not from himself—he knows because he was born of God.
He briefly retells how an angel stopped him from destroying the church, speaking face to face with a voice like thunder that shook the earth.
He suffered three days of anguish and found no forgiveness until he cried to the Lord Jesus Christ for mercy—and then found peace.

f.g: Forgiveness of sins.

f.w: I did find peace to my soul

chapters.n: The lesson: there is no other way to be saved except in and through Christ. He is the life and light of the world and the word of truth.

f.w: no other way or means whereby man can be saved
the life and the light of the world

chapters.n: Shiblon should keep teaching and be diligent and temperate—balanced and self-controlled—in everything.

f.g: Moderate and self-controlled.

chapters.n: Avoid pride. Don’t boast of your own wisdom or strength.
Be bold but not domineering. “Bridle” your passions—guide and control them as a bridle guides a horse—so you can be filled with love. Avoid idleness.

f.g: A bridle steers a horse; it channels its strength rather than killing it.
Domineering, pushy behavior.

chapters.n: Don’t pray like the Zoramites, who prayed to be heard and praised by others.

Instead of thanking God that you’re better than others, ask forgiveness for your own unworthiness and pray for mercy on your brethren. This echoes Jesus’ parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector.

f.w: I thank thee that we are better than our brethren

chapters.n: Alma blesses Shiblon that the Lord will receive him into His kingdom in peace, sends him to teach, urges him to be sober, and bids him farewell.
Alma turns to his youngest son, Corianton, with more to say. He points to Shiblon’s steady, faithful example and asks whether it hasn’t set a good pattern for Corianton.
Corianton didn’t listen to his father as well as Shiblon did during the Zoramite mission. He started boasting in his own strength and wisdom.
Worse, Corianton abandoned his mission and went to Siron, near Lamanite lands, to pursue a prostitute named Isabel. This deeply grieved his father.

f.g: A prostitute.

chapters.n: Isabel led many astray, but Alma tells Corianton that’s no excuse. He should have stayed focused on the work entrusted to him.
Alma teaches the seriousness of sexual sin: in God’s eyes it is more abominable than any sin except murder and denying the Holy Ghost. Sacred powers of creation are meant for marriage.

f.g: Something God regards as deeply offensive.

chapters.n: Denying the Holy Ghost after having received it and knowing what one is doing is unforgivable. Murder against the light of God is also very hard to be forgiven.
Alma wishes Corianton had never committed so serious a sin. He wouldn’t bring it up at all if it weren’t for Corianton’s good.

f.g: Stir up deep distress, as a harrow tears up soil.

chapters.n: Sins can’t be hidden from God. Unless they are repented of, they will testify against a person at the final judgment.

f.w: ye cannot hide your crimes from God

chapters.n: Alma pleads with Corianton to repent, forsake his sins, stop following the “lusts of his eyes,” and “cross himself”—deny himself these desires. Without this he cannot inherit God’s kingdom.

f.g: Deny yourself; resist your own desires.

chapters.n: Corianton is to counsel with his older brothers, Helaman and Shiblon. Being young, he needs their support and should heed their advice.
Don’t let vain or foolish things lead you away again. Corianton’s behavior had a painful consequence: the Zoramites saw it and refused to believe Alma’s message.

f.w: when they saw your conduct they would not believe

chapters.n: The Spirit tells Alma to command his children to do good so they don’t lead others to destruction. So he solemnly commands Corianton to stop his sins.

f.g: With reverent seriousness before God.

chapters.n: Turn to the Lord with all your mind, might, and strength. Lead no one else into sin; go back to the people, admit your faults, and try to make it right.

f.w: with all your mind, might, and strength

chapters.n: Don’t chase wealth or worldly things—you can’t take them with you.

f.w: you cannot carry them with you

chapters.n: Alma moves from rebuke to hope. Christ will surely come to take away the sins of the world—including Corianton’s—and bring glad tidings of salvation.

f.w: take away the sins of the world

f.g: Good news—the gospel.

chapters.n: That message was exactly what Corianton had been called to preach: preparing the people—and their children—for Christ’s coming.
Corianton apparently wondered why Christ’s coming should be announced so far in advance. Alma answers: isn’t a soul today just as precious to God as one living when Christ comes?

f.w: a soul at this time as precious

chapters.n: Doesn’t this generation need to know the plan of redemption as much as their children will?
And isn’t it just as easy for God to send angels with this good news now as later? God loves every generation equally.

f.w: send his angel to declare these glad tidings

chapters.n: Alma senses that Corianton is troubled about the resurrection—how and when the dead will rise—and sets out to explain.
First point: no one will be resurrected until after Christ comes. Mortal bodies do not become immortal until He opens the way.

f.w: this mortal does not put on immortality

f.g: Decay; the mortal body that ages and dies.

chapters.n: Christ brings about the resurrection, but it hasn’t happened yet. Many mysteries are known only to God, but Alma has earnestly asked God about this one topic and will share what he learned.

f.w: he bringeth to pass the resurrection

chapters.n: There is a set time when everyone will rise from the dead. Only God knows when.
Whether the dead rise all at once or in several stages doesn’t matter to Alma. What matters is that everyone will rise. Modeling humility, he separates what he knows from what he doesn’t.
Logically, there must be a gap between death and resurrection.

f.g: Between.

chapters.n: So what happens to people’s spirits during that gap? That is Alma’s question.
People die at different times, and with God all time is like one day—time is something only mortals measure.

f.w: all is as one day with God

chapters.n: Alma restates: there’s a set time for the resurrection and a space before it. What happens to souls in that space is what he asked the Lord and now knows.
When the resurrection comes, everyone will see that God knew all the appointed times.

An angel taught Alma that at death every spirit, good or evil, is “taken home to that God who gave them life.” This likely means returning to God’s realm and power, not necessarily into His immediate presence.

f.w: taken home to that God who gave them life

chapters.n: The spirits of the righteous enter paradise—a state of happiness, rest, and peace, free from trouble, care, and sorrow.
The spirits of the wicked, who chose evil and let the devil take possession of them, are cast into “outer darkness,” with weeping and grinding of teeth—the result of their own choices.

f.g: Grinding the teeth in anguish or rage.

chapters.n: The wicked remain in darkness, fearfully anticipating God’s judgment, while the righteous stay in paradise—both until the resurrection.

f.w: fearful looking for the fiery indignation

chapters.n: Some call this assignment of spirits to happiness or misery a “first resurrection.” Alma grants it could be called a raising of the spirit in a loose sense.

f.g: Assignment or delivery to a place or condition.

chapters.n: Prophets also spoke of a first resurrection for everyone who lived up to the time of Christ’s resurrection.
But Alma says that first resurrection can’t simply mean spirits going to happiness or misery.
It means the literal reuniting of spirit and body, for those from Adam’s day until Christ’s resurrection.

f.w: the reuniting of the soul with the body

chapters.n: Alma won’t say whether all of these—righteous and wicked—rise at the same moment. He only says they rise before those who die after Christ’s resurrection.
Alma carefully labels this as his opinion: the righteous will be resurrected at the time of Christ’s resurrection and ascension.

f.w: I give it as my opinion

chapters.n: Whatever the exact timing, he is sure of this: there is a waiting period in happiness or misery, then a resurrection when soul and body reunite and stand before God to be judged by their works.
This reuniting fulfills the “restoration” the prophets spoke of.
A powerful promise: soul and body will be reunited, every limb and joint restored, not even a hair lost. Everything returns to its proper and perfect form.

f.w: every limb and joint shall be restored

f.g: Bodily form.

chapters.n: This physical restoration is what the prophets meant.
Then the righteous will shine in God’s kingdom.
The wicked, however, face an “awful death”—a spiritual death. Being unclean, they cannot enter God’s kingdom; they reap what they have sown and drink a bitter cup to its dregs.

f.w: no unclean thing can inherit the kingdom of God

f.g: The bitter sediment at the bottom of a cup.

chapters.n: Alma addresses the word “restoration.” Some had twisted the scriptures on this point, and Corianton was confused too—perhaps hoping it meant everyone ends up happy regardless of how they live.

f.g: Twisted or distorted the meaning of.

chapters.n: Restoration is required by God’s justice: everything must return to its proper order. Through Christ’s resurrection, the soul is restored to the body, and every part of the body to its place.

f.g: Required; necessary.

f.w: the soul of man should be restored to its body

chapters.n: Justice also requires judgment by works. If someone’s actions and heart’s desires were good, they will be restored to good at the last day.
If their works were evil, evil is restored to them. All are raised to immortality—some to endless happiness in God’s kingdom, others to endless misery in the devil’s.
Each receives according to what they desired: happiness to those who wanted happiness and goodness, evil to those who wanted evil. Whoever chose evil all day reaps evil “when the night cometh.”
On the other hand, those who repented and desired righteousness to the end will be rewarded with righteousness. Repentance changes what is restored.
These are the Lord’s redeemed, rescued from the endless night of darkness. People are, in a real sense, their own judges, because they choose good or evil.
God’s decrees don’t change, so the way is open: anyone who chooses to walk in it can be saved.
Alma urges Corianton not to risk any more sin by leaning on misunderstood doctrine, as he had before.
One of the Book of Mormon’s most quoted lines: restoration doesn’t mean going from sin to happiness, because “wickedness never was happiness.”
Everyone in a natural, carnal state—living by appetites without God—is in bitterness and chained by sin. They act against God’s nature, which is also against the nature of happiness.
Alma asks: does restoration mean putting something into a state opposite its nature? Of course not.
Restoration means getting back what you gave: evil for evil, carnal for carnal—and good for good, righteous for righteous, just for just, merciful for merciful.

f.w: merciful for that which is merciful

chapters.n: So be merciful to others, deal fairly, judge righteously, and keep doing good. Then mercy, justice, fair judgment, and goodness will be restored to you.
What you send out returns to you. So, rightly understood, the doctrine of restoration condemns the unrepentant sinner rather than excusing him.

f.w: that which ye do send out shall return unto you again

chapters.n: Corianton has one more worry: it seems unfair for God to punish sinners with misery. Alma sets out to explain how justice and mercy work together.

f.g: Assigned or handed over.

chapters.n: Alma starts in Eden. After Adam and Eve were sent out to till the ground, God placed cherubim and a flaming sword east of the garden to guard the tree of life.

f.g: Heavenly beings who guard sacred places.

chapters.n: Having eaten the fruit of knowledge, Adam and Eve now knew good and evil. God kept them from the tree of life so they would not eat it and live forever in their fallen state.

f.w: the man had become as God, knowing good and evil

chapters.n: The result: humanity received time to repent—a “probationary time” to turn to God and serve Him.

f.g: A testing period in which to prove oneself.

chapters.n: Had Adam eaten from the tree of life immediately, he would have lived forever in his sins with no chance to repent, and God’s plan of salvation would have been defeated.

f.g: Defeated; made useless.

chapters.n: Instead, humans were appointed to die. Cut off from the tree of life, they would one day be cut off from the earth, and became “fallen man.”

f.w: it was appointed unto man to die

chapters.n: Adam and Eve were cut off from God physically (they would die) and spiritually (separated from His presence). They now had to follow their own will—agency in a fallen world.

f.w: cut off both temporally and spiritually

chapters.n: It wasn’t wise to rescue them from physical death right away, because mortality is a necessary part of the “great plan of happiness.”
But since the soul never dies and the Fall brought spiritual death—separation from God—it was necessary for humanity to be rescued from that spiritual death.
