Because humans became carnal, sensual, and devilish by nature, this life became a preparatory state—a time to get ready to meet God.
Without the plan of redemption, every soul at death would be miserable, permanently cut off from the Lord.
Humans had no way to rescue themselves from this fallen state, which their own disobedience had brought.
Justice requires that redemption come only on the condition of repentance during this life. Otherwise, mercy would destroy justice—and if justice were destroyed, God would cease to be God.

f.w: God would cease to be God

chapters.n: So all humanity was fallen and held in the grip of justice, which demanded permanent separation from God.
The heart of the chapter: mercy required an atonement, so God Himself atones for the world’s sins. That way justice is satisfied and God can be both perfectly just and merciful.

f.w: God himself atoneth for the sins of the world

chapters.n: Repentance only means something if there is a real consequence. The punishment was made as eternal as the soul, set opposite the plan of happiness, which is also eternal.

f.g: Attached; set in place.

chapters.n: Alma reasons step by step: no repentance without sin, no sin without law, no law without a punishment.

f.w: How could he sin if there was no law?

chapters.n: God set a punishment and a just law, and that law produces a guilty conscience in people who break it.
Example: if there were no law that murderers must die, would anyone fear the penalty for murder?
Likewise, without a law against sin, people wouldn’t fear sinning.
And without law, neither justice nor mercy would have any claim on a person—neither could act at all.

f.g: The created being—a human.

chapters.n: But there is a law, a punishment, and an opportunity to repent. Mercy claims those who repent; justice claims everyone else and carries out the penalty. Otherwise justice would be destroyed and God would not be God.
God remains God: mercy claims the penitent because of the atonement. The atonement brings resurrection, which brings everyone back into God’s presence to be judged by their works.

f.w: the atonement bringeth to pass the resurrection

chapters.n: Justice gets everything it is owed, and mercy claims all that is hers. So only the truly repentant are saved.
Can mercy cheat justice? Not one bit. If it could, God would no longer be God. Christ paid justice in full.

f.g: The smallest amount.

chapters.n: This is how God accomplishes His eternal purposes, prepared before the world began—bringing salvation to some and, by their choice, misery to others.

f.w: from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: Whoever wants to come may freely drink from the waters of life; no one is forced. At the last day, each is restored according to their deeds.

f.w: whosoever will come may come and partake of the waters of life freely

chapters.n: Someone who chose evil and never repented will receive evil, according to God’s law of restoration.
Alma tells Corianton to stop being troubled about God’s fairness. Only let your sins trouble you—in a way that leads you to repent.

f.w: only let your sins trouble you

chapters.n: Don’t deny God’s justice to excuse your sins. Let His justice, mercy, and patience fully govern your heart and humble you to the dust.

f.g: Patience over a long time.

chapters.n: Alma restores Corianton to his calling: go preach with truth and seriousness, bring souls to repentance so mercy can claim them. A later passage shows Corianton did return to the work.

f.w: ye are called of God to preach the word

f.g: Seriousness and self-control.

chapters.n: Alma’s sons go out to preach, including Corianton, now restored to the work. Alma himself can’t rest and goes too.
Mormon briefly notes that they preached by the spirit of prophecy and revelation, under the holy priesthood order by which they were called, then moves on.
Mormon now begins the long war account (chapters 43–62) that he promised earlier, starting in the eighteenth year of the judges (about 74 BC).
The Zoramites have fully joined the Lamanites. Seeing the Lamanites approach, the Nephites gather their armies in Jershon.
Thousands of Lamanites arrive in Antionum under the command of Zerahemnah.

f.g: The Lamanite commander in this campaign; the meta notes he was a Zoramite defector.

chapters.n: Zerahemnah makes Amalekites and Zoramites his chief captains because these Nephite dissenters were more hateful and violent than ordinary Lamanites.
His goal was to keep the Lamanites’ hatred burning so they would serve his own ambitions.
Zerahemnah stirs up anger so he can seize power over the Lamanites and enslave the Nephites—war driven by personal ambition.

f.g: Seize power without right.

chapters.n: The Nephites’ aim is very different: defend their homes, families, rights, and liberty, including the freedom to worship God as they choose.

f.w: worship God according to their desires

chapters.n: They knew that if the Lamanite leaders won, true believers would be destroyed.
They also knew the Lamanites especially hated the people of Ammon, who had covenanted never to fight again and would be slaughtered if captured.

f.w: they had entered into a covenant

chapters.n: The Nephites refused to let the people of Ammon be destroyed and gave them land as an inheritance.
The people of Ammon contributed much of their wealth to support the army. The Nephites fought alone against a coalition of Lamanites and many groups of Nephite dissenters.

f.w: the descendants of the priests of Noah

f.g: Mixture or combination.

chapters.n: These dissenter descendants were nearly as numerous as the Nephites themselves. The Nephites were forced into bloodshed against their own kin.
With the Lamanites massed in Antionum, the Nephite armies wait in Jershon.
The Nephites’ chief captain, commanding all their armies, is named Moroni—not the later prophet Moroni, but the man who may have inspired Mormon to name his son.
Moroni takes full command of the war effort at just twenty-five years old.
He meets the Lamanites at Jershon’s borders with men armed with swords, cimeters, and other weapons.

f.g: Scimitars—curved swords.

chapters.n: Moroni’s innovation: his soldiers wear breastplates, arm-shields, head protection, and thick clothing. Defensive armor was new to these armies.
Zerahemnah’s army has swords, cimeters, bows, stones, and slings, but most wear only loincloths. Only the Zoramite and Amalekite officers are clothed.

f.g: Wrapped around their waist.

chapters.n: Lacking armor, the Lamanites are terrified of the protected Nephites, even though they greatly outnumber them.
Afraid to attack, the Lamanites slip into the wilderness and circle around by the headwaters of the river Sidon, planning to seize Manti while Moroni’s army is elsewhere.

f.g: Dared.

chapters.n: Moroni sends spies to watch them and, trusting Alma’s prophetic gift, also asks Alma to inquire of the Lord where the army should go—combining practical strategy with revelation.
The Lord reveals to Alma that the Lamanites are heading for Manti to attack the weaker part of the people. Messengers bring this word to Moroni.
Moroni leaves part of his army to protect Jershon in case of a surprise attack and marches the rest to Manti.
He rallies all the people of that region to defend their lands, country, rights, and liberties, so they are ready when the Lamanites arrive.
Moroni hides his army in a valley near the west bank of the Sidon.

f.g: Hidden.

chapters.n: He posts spies all around to learn when the Lamanite army will arrive.
Moroni understands the Lamanite leaders’ goal: to destroy or enslave the Nephites and set up their own kingdom over all the land.
Because the Nephites sought only to protect their lands, liberty, and church, Moroni felt it was no sin to defend them with clever tactics.

f.g: A clever plan to trick or outmaneuver an enemy.

chapters.n: He divides his force, hiding part of it on the east and south of the hill Riplah.

f.g: A hill near the river Sidon by Manti; mentioned only in this account.

chapters.n: The rest he hides in the west valley, west of the Sidon, stretching down toward Manti.
With his forces in position, Moroni is ready.
The Lamanites come in north of the hill where part of Moroni’s army is hidden.
As they pass Riplah and begin crossing the Sidon, a hidden force led by Lehi springs out and surrounds them from behind on the east.

f.g: A Nephite captain and trusted friend of Moroni, not Lehi the prophet.

chapters.n: Seeing Nephites at their rear, the Lamanites turn to fight Lehi’s army.
The killing is terrible on both sides but far worse for the unarmored Lamanites, who fall at nearly every blow.
Only an occasional Nephite falls, because armor protects their vital organs. Moroni’s preparation saves many lives.

f.g: Organs essential to life.

chapters.n: Overwhelmed by their losses, the Lamanites panic and flee toward the Sidon.
Lehi drives them across the river but holds his own men on the east bank.
On the other side, Moroni’s army meets them in the valley and attacks.
The Lamanites flee toward Manti, only to run into more of Moroni’s forces.
Cornered, the Lamanites fight harder than they ever had in all their history.
Urged on by their Zoramite and Amalekite captains and by Zerahemnah, they fight “like dragons,” splitting helmets, piercing breastplates, and cutting off arms. Many Nephites die.

f.g: Fierce, monstrous creatures—a figure for savage fighting.

chapters.n: But the Nephites fought for a better cause: not for a king or power, but for homes, liberty, families, everything they had, and their freedom to worship.
They believed defending themselves was a duty to God, who had taught that if they were not guilty of the first or second offense, they should not let themselves be killed by enemies.

f.w: the first offense, neither the second

chapters.n: The Lord had also taught them to defend their families even to the point of bloodshed. That was the reason they fought—for families, lands, country, rights, and religion.

f.w: defend your families even unto bloodshed

chapters.n: Faced with such fury, Moroni’s men begin to waver and are about to run. Moroni reminds them of their lands, their liberty, and freedom from bondage.
They turn back and cry with one voice to the Lord for liberty and freedom.

f.w: cried with one voice unto the Lord

chapters.n: In the very hour they pray, they fight with new power, and the Lamanites flee back to the Sidon.
Although the Lamanites outnumber them more than two to one, they are driven into one mass in the valley by the river.
Moroni’s forces surround them on both sides of the river, with Lehi’s men on the east.
Zerahemnah sees Nephites on both banks and realizes his army is trapped. Terror sets in.
Seeing their terror, Moroni immediately orders his men to stop the killing. His aim was victory and safety, not slaughter.
The Nephites step back. Moroni tells Zerahemnah they don’t want to be “men of blood.” The Lamanites are at their mercy, but Moroni would rather spare them.

f.g: People who love killing.

chapters.n: Moroni contrasts the two sides: the Nephites aren’t fighting for power or to enslave anyone, yet that is exactly why the Lamanites came—and they’re angry over the Nephites’ religion.
Moroni attributes the victory to the Lord and to their faith in Christ, a faith the Lamanites cannot destroy.
This proves theirs is God’s true faith. God will preserve them as long as they stay faithful; only transgression and denying their faith could lead to their destruction.

f.w: except we should fall into transgression

chapters.n: In God’s name, Moroni appeals to everything sacred to the Nephites—faith, worship, church, families, liberty, country, and God’s word, “to which we owe all our happiness.”

f.w: the sacred word of God, to which we owe all our happiness

chapters.n: His terms: surrender your weapons and go home, promising never to return to war, and your lives will be spared.
If they refuse, Moroni will order his men to attack until the Lamanites are wiped out—then everyone will see who ends up in bondage.

f.g: Completely destroyed.

chapters.n: Zerahemnah hands over his sword, cimeter, and bow but refuses to swear an oath he knows he and his people would break. He asks to leave—or else they will fight to the end.
He rejects Moroni’s faith: the Nephites won by cleverness and armor, not God. Faith and preparation, though, are not opposites in Moroni’s view.

f.g: Your cleverness or trickery.

chapters.n: Moroni hands the weapons back. He will not accept a surrender without a covenant of peace, so the fight must be settled.
Moroni can’t take back his word, sworn by the living Lord: they leave only under an oath never to return to war, or they die.

f.g: A solemn oath formula, meaning “as surely as God lives.”

chapters.n: Furious, Zerahemnah charges at Moroni. A Nephite soldier strikes his sword to the ground, breaking it at the hilt, and slices off Zerahemnah’s scalp. Zerahemnah retreats into his ranks.

f.g: The handle of a sword.

chapters.n: The soldier lifts the scalp on the point of his sword and holds it up for all to see.
He warns: just as your chief’s scalp fell to the earth, you will fall unless you surrender your weapons and leave under a covenant of peace.
Many are struck with fear, throw down their weapons at Moroni’s feet, and covenant peace. Those who do are allowed to leave.
Zerahemnah, enraged, stirs up the rest of his soldiers to fight even harder.

f.g: Very angry.

chapters.n: Angry at their stubbornness, Moroni orders the attack to resume, and the Lamanites fight back with all their strength.
Unprotected, the Lamanites fall rapidly before the Nephite swords—just as Moroni’s soldier had warned.
Seeing his army about to be destroyed, Zerahemnah finally cries out to Moroni, promising that he and his people will covenant never to fight them again if spared.
Once again Moroni halts the killing. He takes the Lamanites’ weapons, and after they covenant peace, lets them return to the wilderness.
The dead were too many to count—enormous losses on both sides.
The bodies were thrown into the river Sidon and carried out to the depths of the sea.
Moroni’s army returns home to their houses and lands.
The eighteenth year of the judges ends (about 73 BC), and with it Mormon’s abridgment of the record Alma kept on the plates of Nephi. Helaman’s record begins next.
Mormon begins abridging Helaman’s record. The Nephites rejoice at being delivered again, giving thanks, fasting, praying, and worshipping with great joy.
In the nineteenth year of the judges (about 73 BC), Alma comes to Helaman and asks whether he believes what he was told about the records.
Helaman answers simply: yes, I believe.
Alma asks the most important question: do you believe in Jesus Christ, who is coming?
Helaman affirms he believes everything his father has taught.
Alma asks if he will keep his commandments.
Helaman promises to keep them with all his heart.
Alma blesses him: the Lord will prosper him in the land. This simple interview resembles the commitments asked of people before receiving sacred responsibilities.
Alma now gives a prophecy that Helaman must write down but keep secret until it is fulfilled.
By revelation, Alma sees that four hundred years after Christ appears to them, the Nephites will fall into unbelief.

f.g: Gradually lose faith.

chapters.n: Wars, plagues, famines, and bloodshed will follow until the Nephites cease to exist as a people.

f.g: Deadly epidemic diseases.

chapters.n: This will happen because they sin against great light and knowledge, falling into secret evils and sexual sin. The fourth generation after Christ’s coming will not all pass before it begins.

f.g: Lustful, sexually immoral behavior.

chapters.n: Soon after that day, the descendants of today’s Nephites will no longer be counted as Nephites.

Survivors will be counted among the Lamanites and become like them, except a few “disciples of the Lord,” whom the Lamanites will hunt until they are gone. Mormon and Moroni witnessed this fulfillment.
Alma blesses Helaman, his other sons, and the earth itself for the sake of the righteous.
The Lord’s word: this land is cursed for any nation that becomes fully ripe in wickedness, because the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least allowance. It is both a blessing and a warning.

f.w: the Lord cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance

chapters.n: Alma blesses the church and all who will stay faithful from then on.
Alma leaves Zarahemla as if heading to Melek and is never heard from again. No one knows of his death or burial.

He was a righteous man. Church members said he was taken up by the Spirit or buried by the Lord like Moses. Mormon supposes the Lord received Alma to Himself; Latter-day Saints understand this as being “translated.”
At the start of the nineteenth year, Helaman goes out preaching among the people.
Because of the wars and many small disputes, it was necessary to preach the word and set the church in order again.

f.g: The church should be reorganized and put in order.

chapters.n: Helaman and his brothers re-establish the church in every Nephite city, appointing priests and teachers over each congregation.
After this, dissension arises, and some refuse to listen to Helaman and his brothers.
The cause is pride from great wealth. They become rich in their own eyes and refuse to walk uprightly before God—a pattern the Book of Mormon repeats often.
Those who rejected Helaman’s preaching band together against their fellow Nephites.
Their anger runs so hot that they are determined to kill the faithful.

f.g: Furious.

chapters.n: Their leader is Amalickiah, a large, strong man.
Amalickiah wants to be king, and his followers—mostly lower judges hungry for power—want him to be king too.
He flattered them with promises: make me king, and I’ll make you rulers over the people.

f.g: Insincere praise used to manipulate.

chapters.n: Despite the high priests’ preaching and care for the church, Amalickiah leads these people into rebellion.
Many church members believe his flattery and leave the church. Even right after a great, God-given victory, Nephite society is now in serious danger.

f.g: Unstable; in danger of collapse.

chapters.n: Mormon’s lesson: how quickly people forget the Lord and are led away by the evil one.

f.w: how quick the children of men do forget

chapters.n: We also see how much harm one very wicked person can cause.
Through cunning and flattery, Amalickiah leads many to seek the destruction of the church and of the liberty God gave the land for the sake of the righteous.

f.g: Clever, deceptive scheming.

chapters.n: When Moroni, the chief commander, hears of this rebellion, he is angry with Amalickiah.
Moroni tears his coat and writes on a piece: “In memory of our God, our religion, and freedom, and our peace, our wives, and our children.” He fastens it to a pole as a banner.

f.g: Tore.

chapters.n: Dressed in full armor, Moroni names the banner “the title of liberty,” bows to the earth, and prays mightily that liberty will bless the land as long as Christians remain there.
Mormon explains that “Christians” was the name outsiders gave to true believers in Christ.
Faithful members gladly took on the name of Christ—“Christians”—because they believed in the Christ who would come, even about seventy years before His birth.

f.w: took upon them, gladly, the name of Christ

chapters.n: So Moroni prays that the Christians’ cause and the freedom of the land would prosper.
After pouring out his soul, Moroni names the whole land, north and south, “a chosen land, and the land of liberty.”
Moroni declares that God will not let those despised for Christ’s name be destroyed—unless they bring it on themselves through their own sins.

f.w: until we bring it upon us by our own transgressions

chapters.n: He goes among the people waving the banner so all can read it, calling out loudly.
His call: whoever will uphold this standard, come in the Lord’s strength and covenant to defend your rights and religion, so God may bless you.
People come running in armor and tear their own clothes as a sign of covenant: if they forsake God or are ashamed of Christ’s name, may the Lord tear them as they tore their garments.

f.g: As a symbol or pledge.

chapters.n: They throw their torn garments at Moroni’s feet, covenanting that if they fall into sin, God may cast them at their enemies’ feet, like the garments being trampled.

f.w: our brethren in the land northward

chapters.n: Moroni reminds them they are a remnant of Jacob and of Joseph, whose coat his brothers tore. If they don’t keep God’s commandments, they too may be torn apart, imprisoned, sold, or killed.

f.w: a remnant of the seed of Joseph

chapters.n: Moroni recounts a tradition, not found in the Bible, that Jacob saw part of Joseph’s coat preserved and prophesied that a remnant of Joseph’s descendants would likewise be preserved by God.
Jacob continued: the loss of part of Joseph’s posterity grieves him, but he rejoices in the part that will be taken to God.
Mormon notes these were Jacob’s own words, likely from the brass plates.
Moroni applies it: perhaps the part of Joseph’s seed that perishes are the dissenters—or it could even be them, if they don’t stand firm in Christ.
Moroni gathers all who want to defend liberty from every troubled region to stand against Amalickiah and his followers, now called Amalickiahites.
Seeing he’s outnumbered and his followers doubt their cause, Amalickiah takes those willing and flees toward the land of Nephi.
Moroni doesn’t want the Lamanites strengthened. Knowing Amalickiah will stir them to war, he plans to intercept the group and bring them back.

f.g: Wise or advisable.

chapters.n: So Moroni marches his newly covenanted army into the wilderness to cut off Amalickiah’s route.
Moroni gets ahead of Amalickiah’s forces in the wilderness.

f.g: Got in front of; cut off.

chapters.n: Amalickiah escapes with a few men; the rest are captured and taken back to Zarahemla.
Moroni had been appointed by the chief judges and the voice of the people, so he had legal authority over the armies.
Amalickiahites who refused to covenant to support a free government were put to death. In wartime, this was treated as treason. Few refused.
Moroni has the title of liberty raised on every tower in Nephite lands, planting the standard of freedom everywhere.

f.g: A flag or banner marking a rallying point.

chapters.n: Peace returns and lasts until nearly the end of the nineteenth year.
Helaman and the high priests keep order in the church, which enjoys four years of peace and rejoicing.
Many die firmly believing that Christ has redeemed their souls, leaving the world with joy.

f.w: redeemed by the Lord Jesus Christ

chapters.n: Some die of seasonal fevers, but fewer than might be expected because of medicinal plants and roots God had provided against illnesses common in that climate.
Many die of old age, and those who die faithful in Christ are, as Mormon supposes, happy in Him.
Mormon returns to Amalickiah, who has fled to the Lamanites in the land of Nephi. He stirs them to anger, and the Lamanite king proclaims a call to war against the Nephites.

f.w: fled with him into the wilderness

chapters.n: The Lamanites are caught between two fears: angering their king, and dying in another war with the Nephites after their recent defeat. Most refuse to obey.

f.w: lest they should lose their lives

chapters.n: The angry king gives Amalickiah command of the loyal troops, ordering him to force the others to take up arms.

f.g: Force them to join the army.

chapters.n: This is exactly what Amalickiah wanted. Being cunning in evil, he secretly plans to overthrow the king.

f.g: Crafty; sly.

chapters.n: Commanding the king’s loyalists, he sets out to win over the rebels, who have fled in fear to Onidah, their place of arms.

f.g: A Lamanite gathering place; not the same as the hill Onidah among the Zoramites (Alma 32:4).

chapters.n: The rebels have chosen their own king and leader, firmly resolved not to be forced into war against the Nephites.
They gather on top of Mount Antipas, ready to fight.

f.g: A mountain in Lamanite territory; not to be confused with the Nephite commander Antipus.

chapters.n: Amalickiah has no plan to fight them. He wants to win the army’s loyalty, put himself at its head, and take the throne.
He camps his army in the valley near the mountain.
At night, he secretly sends messengers asking the rebel leader, Lehonti, to come down to meet him.

f.g: A group of messengers or envoys.

chapters.n: Lehonti is wary and refuses. Amalickiah asks a second and third time.

f.g: Dared.

chapters.n: Unable to coax him down, Amalickiah climbs almost to Lehonti’s camp and sends a fourth invitation, telling him to bring his guards—making the meeting seem safe.
Amalickiah offers a deal: surround my troops by night, and I’ll hand them over to you—if you make me your second-in-command.
Lehonti agrees and surrounds Amalickiah’s men before dawn.
Waking to find themselves surrounded, Amalickiah’s soldiers beg to join their brethren rather than be killed—just what Amalickiah wanted.
He hands over his men, directly disobeying the king, as one more step toward seizing the throne.
Mormon explains a key detail: by Lamanite custom, if the chief leader died, the second leader took his place.
Amalickiah has a servant poison Lehonti little by little until he dies—a slow, hidden murder.

f.g: Gradually, a little at a time.

chapters.n: With Lehonti dead, the Lamanites make Amalickiah their commander.
Having achieved his aim, Amalickiah marches the combined army to the city of Nephi, the Lamanite capital.
The king comes out with his guards to greet him, believing Amalickiah has obeyed orders and gathered a great army for war.
Amalickiah sends servants ahead, who bow before the king as if honoring him.
The king reaches out to lift them up—a Lamanite custom of peace borrowed from the Nephites.

f.g: A gesture showing friendship.

chapters.n: As he lifts the first servant, that servant stabs the king in the heart. The very gesture of peace becomes the moment of betrayal.

f.w: stabbed the king to the heart

chapters.n: The king’s own servants run in terror, and Amalickiah’s servants raise a cry.
They falsely accuse the king’s servants of killing him, pointing to their flight as evidence.
Amalickiah marches his army to the scene, finds the king in his blood, fakes outrage, and calls everyone who loved the king to hunt down the “murderers.”

f.g: Blood from a wound.

chapters.n: All who loved the king chase after the innocent servants.
Terrified, the king’s servants flee to Zarahemla and join the people of Ammon—finding refuge among converted Lamanites.
The pursuers return empty-handed, and through this deception Amalickiah wins the people’s hearts.

f.g: Deliberate deception for gain.

chapters.n: The next day he takes possession of the city of Nephi.
Amalickiah sends word to the queen that her husband was killed by his own servants, who escaped despite pursuit.
The queen asks him to spare the city, to come see her, and to bring witnesses about the king’s death.
Brazenly, Amalickiah brings the actual killer and his companions as “witnesses.” They swear the king’s servants did it, citing their flight, and the queen is convinced.
Amalickiah wins the queen’s favor and marries her. Through fraud and his servants’ help he becomes king over all the Lamanites, including the many descendants of Nephite dissenters.

f.w: took her unto him to wife
f.g: Married her.

chapters.n: Mormon observes a sad irony: Nephite dissenters, who had known the Lord, soon became more hardened and fierce than the Lamanites, adopting their traditions, idleness, and immorality, and forgetting God entirely.

f.g: Laziness.

chapters.n: As soon as he becomes king, Amalickiah uses propaganda—men preaching from towers—to stir up Lamanite hatred against the Nephites.

f.g: High platforms used for public speaking or watching.

chapters.n: By late in the nineteenth year (about 72 BC), Amalickiah is no longer content with ruling the Lamanites; he wants to rule the Nephites too.
He has hardened Lamanite hearts, blinded their minds, and assembled a huge army for war.
Confident in his numbers, he means to overpower the Nephites and enslave them.
He appoints Zoramites as chief captains because, as former Nephites, they know Nephite strength, hiding places, and weak points.

f.g: Places of refuge or defense.

chapters.n: The Lamanite army breaks camp and moves through the wilderness toward Zarahemla.
A deliberate contrast: while Amalickiah gained power through fraud, Moroni was preparing his people spiritually to be faithful to God.

f.w: preparing the minds of the people

chapters.n: Moroni also strengthens the army and builds small forts, earthen banks, and stone walls around cities and borders throughout the land.
He stations the most men at the weakest fortifications, wisely balancing the land’s defenses.
All this is to defend liberty, land, families, and peace so the people can live for God and keep what their enemies called “the cause of Christians.”
Mormon’s tribute begins: Moroni was strong and mighty, of “perfect understanding,” took no pleasure in bloodshed, and rejoiced in freedom for his people.

f.g: Complete, mature understanding—sound and wise judgment.

chapters.n: His heart overflowed with gratitude to God for his people’s blessings, and he worked tirelessly for their welfare and safety.
He was firm in the faith of Christ and had sworn to defend his people, rights, country, and religion, even with his life.
The Nephite ethic of war: defend yourselves, even to bloodshed if necessary, but never be the aggressor or raise the sword except to preserve life.
They believed that if they kept God’s commandments, He would prosper them and warn them whether to flee or prepare for war.
They also trusted God to tell them where to defend themselves, as He did through Alma. Moroni gloried not in bloodshed but in doing good, protecting his people, and resisting evil.

f.w: make it known unto them whither they should go

chapters.n: One of the Book of Mormon’s great tributes: if everyone were like Moroni, the powers of hell would be shaken forever and the devil would lose his power over human hearts.

f.w: the very powers of hell would have been shaken forever

chapters.n: Mormon ranks Moroni with Ammon, the other sons of Mosiah, and Alma and his sons—all men of God.
Helaman and his brothers served the people just as valuably by preaching and baptizing all who would listen. Soldiers and preachers both mattered.
Because the people humbled themselves, the Lord favored them, and they had four years free from internal conflict.
Even so, at the end of the nineteenth year they were forced, against their will, into war with the Lamanites.
In fact, wars with the Lamanites continued for many years despite the Nephites’ reluctance.
The Nephites grieved at having to fight. They hated bloodshed and were especially sorrowful to send so many of their brethren into eternity unprepared to meet God.
Still, they could not just lay down their lives and let their families be massacred by former brethren who had dissented and joined the Lamanites.

f.g: Savagely cruel.

chapters.n: They would not let the dissenters triumph while any remained who kept God’s commandments, trusting the Lord’s promise that the obedient would prosper in the land.

f.w: they should prosper in the land

chapters.n: On the tenth day of the eleventh month of the nineteenth year, Lamanite armies are seen approaching Ammonihah.
Ammonihah had been rebuilt, and Moroni stationed an army there behind earthen walls that protected against Lamanite arrows and stones.
The city was only partly rebuilt. Since the Lamanites had destroyed it once before because of its wickedness, they expected another easy victory.
To their dismay, a high ridge of earth surrounds the defenders. Missiles can’t reach them, and the only way in is through a single entrance.
The Lamanite chief captains are amazed at the Nephites’ clever defensive preparations.
The Lamanites had expected their numbers to win, and they had even copied Moroni’s idea of armor, with shields, breastplates, and thick skin garments.
So equipped, they assumed they could easily enslave or massacre the Nephites at will.
But the Nephites were prepared in a way never before seen among Lehi’s descendants, following Moroni’s instructions.
The Lamanites—here called Amalickiahites—are stunned by these preparations.
Mormon suggests that if Amalickiah had led in person, he might have forced an attack anyway, since he didn’t care how many of his own soldiers died.
But Amalickiah stayed home, and his captains didn’t dare attack. Moroni had changed the whole way the Nephites defended themselves.

f.g: Dared.

chapters.n: So the Lamanites withdraw into the wilderness and march toward Noah, assuming it is the next best target.
Unaware that Moroni had fortified every city, they march on Noah, and the captains swear an oath to destroy its people.
To their shock, Noah—once a weak point—is now even stronger than Ammonihah.
This was Moroni’s plan: he expected them to be scared off by Ammonihah and to turn to Noah, the former weak spot, so he strengthened it most.
Moroni put Lehi in command at Noah—the same captain who had fought the Lamanites east of the Sidon.
The Lamanites greatly fear Lehi, but because their captains swore an oath, they press the attack anyway.
The high bank and deep ditch mean the only way into the fort is the entrance.
Defenders are ready to hurl stones and arrows at anyone trying to climb over.
The strongest Nephite men, with swords and slings, guard the entrance against all who try to force their way in.
The Lamanite captains attack the entrance repeatedly and are driven back each time with enormous losses.

Unable to break through the pass, they try to dig down the earthen banks, but are cut down by stones and arrows. Instead of filling the ditches with dirt, they fill them with their own dead and wounded.
The Nephites hold complete control. All the Lamanite chief captains are killed, along with over a thousand soldiers, while not one Nephite dies.

f.w: not a single soul of the Nephites which was slain

chapters.n: About fifty Nephites are wounded by arrows through the entrance, but their armor protects vital areas, so the wounds are on their legs—some serious.
With their leaders dead, the Lamanites flee home to report to Amalickiah, who Mormon notes was a Nephite by birth.
Amalickiah is furious that he has failed to bring the Nephites into bondage.
He curses God and Moroni and swears to drink Moroni’s blood—all because Moroni had obeyed God in preparing to protect his people.
The Nephites, meanwhile, thank the Lord for His matchless power in delivering them.
So ends the nineteenth year of the judges.

Peace and great prosperity in the church follow, because the people heeded the word preached by Helaman, Shiblon, Corianton, Ammon and his brothers, and others called by the holy order of God. Note that Corianton is again serving faithfully.
Moroni keeps preparing even in peacetime. Starting in the twentieth year of the judges (about 72 BC), his armies pile up earthen ridges around every Nephite city.
On top of the earthen ridges, they build timber walls about as tall as a man.
On the timbers they add a strong, high frame of pickets—a sharpened-stake fence.

f.g: Pointed stakes forming a fence or palisade.

chapters.n: Towers overlook these walls, with protected shelters on top so defenders are safe from Lamanite stones and arrows.
From the towers, defenders can hurl stones at anyone approaching the walls.
In this way Moroni builds strongholds around every city in the land.

f.g: Fortified places.

chapters.n: Moroni’s armies clear the Lamanites out of the east wilderness, driving them back to their own lands south of Zarahemla.
Mormon adds a geographic note: the land of Nephi stretched in a straight line from the east sea to the west sea.

f.w: the east sea to the west

chapters.n: With the east wilderness cleared, Moroni has Nephite settlers move there, all the way to the seashore, to occupy and hold the land.
He also posts armies along the southern border and has them build fortifications to protect soldiers and civilians.

He eliminates Lamanite strongholds in the east and west, fortifying the whole boundary between Zarahemla and Nephi from the west sea past the head of the river Sidon. The Nephites hold all the land to the north.
Moroni’s army grows daily because his defenses give people confidence. His goal is to strip the Lamanites of any power over Nephite lands.
The Nephites found a new city named Moroni by the east sea, on the southern border with the Lamanites.
They also found the city and land of Nephihah between the cities of Moroni and Aaron, named after the chief judge.
That year they begin many cities in the north, notably one called Lehi near the seashore.
So ends the twentieth year of the judges—a year spent not in battle but in building defenses and new cities.
The Nephites enter the twenty-first year in these prosperous conditions.
They prosper greatly, grow very rich, and multiply and become strong.

f.g: Grow strong.

chapters.n: Mormon draws a lesson: the Lord’s dealings are merciful and just, and His words to Lehi are being fulfilled.

f.g: His words are proven true.

chapters.n: The promise to Lehi: obedience brings prosperity in the land; disobedience brings separation from the Lord.

f.w: they shall prosper in the land

chapters.n: Mormon observes that the Nephites’ wars and destructions came from their own sins—quarrels, murders, plunder, idolatry, and immorality.

f.g: Worship of idols or anything placed above God.

chapters.n: The faithful were always delivered, while thousands of the wicked ended up in bondage, dead, or lost in unbelief among the Lamanites.
A remarkable statement: there had never been a happier time among the Nephites since Nephi’s day than in Moroni’s day, in this twenty-first year.

f.w: there never was a happier time

chapters.n: The twenty-second and twenty-third years also pass in peace.
Peace would have continued in the twenty-fourth year except for a land dispute between Lehi and neighboring Morianton, both near the sea.
The people of Morianton claim part of Lehi’s land. The quarrel grows heated, and Morianton’s people take up arms, determined to kill their neighbors.
The people of Lehi flee to Moroni’s camp for help—and they were in the right.
The leader of Morianton’s people, also named Morianton, fears Moroni’s army will come to destroy them.
So Morianton persuades his people to flee to the land northward, a land of many waters, and take it over.
This plan would have caused great trouble, but Morianton, a man of violent temper, beats one of his maidservants badly.

f.g: Deeply regretted.
A man with an uncontrolled temper.

chapters.n: She escapes to Moroni’s camp and tells him everything, including the plan to flee north. Her courage changes the course of events.
Moroni fears Morianton will unite with the people of Bountiful and seize those northern lands, a move that could eventually overthrow Nephite liberty.
So Moroni sends an army to cut them off and stop their flight north.

f.g: Get ahead of; intercept.

chapters.n: The army doesn’t catch them until the borders of Desolation, at the narrow pass by the sea leading to the land northward.
The army is led by Teancum. Morianton’s people, stirred by his flattery, fight stubbornly; Teancum kills Morianton, defeats his army, and brings back prisoners. So ends the twenty-fourth year.
After covenanting peace, Morianton’s people return to their land, reconcile with the people of Lehi, and both groups receive their lands back.
That same year, Nephihah, the second chief judge, dies after serving with complete integrity before God.
Mormon notes that Nephihah had declined Alma’s offer to keep the sacred records, so Alma gave them to Helaman.

f.w: conferred them upon his son, Helaman

chapters.n: Nephihah’s son is appointed chief judge and governor, swearing a sacred oath to judge righteously, keep peace and freedom, protect religious liberty, uphold God’s cause, and bring the wicked to justice.
His name is Pahoran. He takes his father’s seat at the end of the twenty-fourth year. He will play a major role in the crises ahead.
The twenty-fifth year of the judges (about 67 BC) begins peacefully, with the land dispute between Lehi and Morianton settled.

f.w: the people of Lehi and the people of Morianton

chapters.n: But peace doesn’t last. A faction wants certain points of the law changed and grows contentious toward the new chief judge, Pahoran.
Pahoran refuses to change the law or allow it to be changed, and ignores their petitions.

f.g: Formal written requests.

chapters.n: Angry, the group wants Pahoran removed. A heated dispute follows, though no blood is shed—yet.
Those who want Pahoran removed are called “king-men,” because their real aim is to overthrow the free government and set up a king.
Pahoran’s supporters call themselves “freemen,” having covenanted to defend their rights and religious freedom through a free government.

f.g: Supporters of the free government of judges.

chapters.n: The dispute is settled by the people’s vote, which favors the freemen. Pahoran keeps his seat, and the king-men are silenced and forced to support freedom—for now.
The king-men were people of “high birth” who wanted to be kings, backed by others hungry for power.

f.g: Aristocratic or noble family background.

chapters.n: Their timing is dangerous: Amalickiah is again rousing the Lamanites, arming soldiers everywhere, and still bent on his oath to drink Moroni’s blood.

f.w: he had sworn to drink the blood of Moroni

chapters.n: Mormon hints that this oath will prove reckless. Still, Amalickiah prepares his armies for war.

f.g: Reckless; made without thinking.

chapters.n: His forces are smaller after the many thousands killed in earlier battles, but he has still raised a huge army and isn’t afraid to march on Zarahemla.
This time Amalickiah leads in person. His invasion comes just as the Nephites are settling the controversy over Pahoran.
The king-men are glad to hear of the invasion and refuse to fight—so angry at the chief judge and the freemen that they won’t defend their own country.
Moroni is furious at the stubbornness of people he has worked so hard to protect, especially as the enemy reaches the borders.
With the people’s support, Moroni petitions the governor for authority to compel the dissenters to defend their country or face death.

f.g: Pahoran, the chief judge.

chapters.n: Moroni’s priority is to end internal strife, which had caused all their past destruction. The people’s voice grants his request.

f.w: this had been hitherto a cause of all their destruction

chapters.n: Moroni orders his army against the king-men to humble their pride and claims of nobility, or force them to take up arms for liberty.
When the king-men raise their weapons against Moroni’s army, they are cut down.

f.g: Cut down.

chapters.n: Four thousand dissenters die. Surviving leaders are imprisoned because there is no time for trials during the crisis.
The rest submit, raise the title of liberty on their towers and cities, and take up arms for their country.
The king-men cease to exist as a group. Those who claimed noble blood are humbled and fight bravely for freedom alongside their brethren.

f.g: Name or title.

chapters.n: While Moroni is dealing with this internal rebellion, the Lamanites invade the land of Moroni on the eastern seashore. The king-men’s delay has cost the Nephites dearly.
The city of Moroni is too weakly defended. Amalickiah drives the Nephites out, kills many, and seizes the city and its fortifications.
Refugees flee to Nephihah, while the people of Lehi prepare for battle.
Amalickiah avoids attacking Nephihah, keeping his army along the coast and garrisoning each captured city.
He takes city after city along the east coast: Nephihah, Lehi, Morianton, Omner, Gid, and Mulek.
The bitter irony: these cities were fortified Moroni’s way, and now they serve as strongholds for the Lamanites.
The Lamanites push to the borders of Bountiful, driving the Nephites and killing many.
There they meet Teancum, the commander who had stopped Morianton.
Teancum cuts off Amalickiah’s march toward Bountiful and the land northward.
Teancum’s men are elite warriors, stronger and more skilled than the Lamanites, and they drive Amalickiah back.
They harass the Lamanites until dark. Teancum camps at the borders of Bountiful, and Amalickiah camps on the beach.
That night Teancum and a servant slip into the Lamanite camp. Exhausted from the day’s heat and fighting, the soldiers are fast asleep.

Teancum sneaks into the king’s tent and drives a javelin through Amalickiah’s heart, killing him so quickly that his servants never wake. Amalickiah, who swore to drink Moroni’s blood, dies on the eve of the new year.

f.g: A light throwing spear.
Secretly.

chapters.n: Teancum returns secretly, wakes his men, and tells them what he has done.
He keeps his army ready in case the Lamanites wake and attack.
So ends the twenty-fifth year—and the life of Amalickiah. His “rash” oath has come to nothing.
On New Year’s morning of the twenty-sixth year (about 66 BC), the Lamanites wake to find Amalickiah dead in his tent and Teancum ready to fight.
Frightened, they give up their march north and retreat into the fortified city of Mulek.
Amalickiah’s brother Ammoron is made king in his place.
Ammoron orders his forces to hold the captured cities, which had cost the Lamanites much blood to take.
Seeing their determination and huge numbers, Teancum judges it unwise to attack the fortified cities.

f.g: Wise or advisable.

chapters.n: Instead he keeps his men nearby, appearing ready for battle while actually building walls and defensive positions.

f.g: Places of refuge or defense.

chapters.n: He continues preparing until Moroni sends reinforcements.
Moroni orders Teancum to keep all Lamanite prisoners, to exchange later for Nephites the Lamanites had captured.

f.g: Something exchanged to free captives.

chapters.n: Moroni also tells him to fortify Bountiful and secure the narrow pass to the land northward, so the Lamanites can’t surround them.
He urges Teancum to hold that region faithfully, strike the Lamanites whenever possible, retake lost cities by strategy or other means, and strengthen cities not yet captured.

f.g: To strike or punish severely.
A clever military plan.

chapters.n: Moroni explains he can’t come himself, because Lamanites are attacking on the west coast and he must face them.
King Ammoron has informed the queen of his brother’s death, gathered a large army, and marched against the Nephites on the west coast.
His strategy: attack in the west to draw Nephite forces away, while troops holding the eastern cities keep up pressure and seize more land.

f.g: To trouble with repeated attacks.

chapters.n: So the twenty-sixth year ends with the Nephites in danger on two fronts.
In the twenty-seventh year, Moroni secures the southern and western borders and begins marching toward Bountiful to help Teancum retake the lost cities.
Teancum is ordered to attack Mulek and retake it if possible.
Teancum prepares but sees he can’t overpower the Lamanites inside their fortifications, so he withdraws to Bountiful to await Moroni.
Moroni arrives in Bountiful late in the twenty-seventh year.
Early in the twenty-eighth year, Moroni, Teancum, and other captains hold a council of war to find a way to lure the Lamanites out of their strongholds and retake Mulek.

f.w: flatter them out of their strongholds
f.g: Entice or trick them into leaving their fortifications.

chapters.n: They invite the Lamanite commander at Mulek, a Zoramite named Jacob, to fight on the open plains, but he refuses.

f.g: Not to be confused with Nephi’s brother Jacob; this is a Lamanite commander.

chapters.n: With no hope of a fair fight, Moroni devises a plan to decoy the Lamanites out.

f.g: To lure into a trap.

chapters.n: Teancum takes a small force along the seashore while Moroni’s army marches at night through the wilderness west of Mulek. In the morning, Lamanite guards spot Teancum and report to Jacob.
Thinking his large army can easily crush Teancum’s small band, Jacob marches out. Teancum retreats northward along the shore.
The Lamanites pursue eagerly. Meanwhile Moroni sends part of his army into the city to take it.
They kill the remaining guards who refuse to surrender their weapons.
Moroni now holds Mulek with part of his army and marches the rest out to meet the Lamanites as they return.
The Lamanites chase Teancum almost to Bountiful, where they meet Lehi and a small army left to guard that city.
Seeing Lehi’s fresh troops, the tired Lamanite captains flee in confusion, trying to reach Mulek before Lehi catches them.
They have no idea Moroni is behind them; they only fear Lehi.
Lehi deliberately doesn’t catch them until they run into Moroni.
Before getting far, the exhausted Lamanites are trapped between Moroni’s and Lehi’s fresh, strong armies.
Moroni orders his men to attack until the Lamanites surrender their weapons.
Jacob, a Zoramite with an unconquerable spirit, leads a furious charge against Moroni.
Since Moroni blocks the way to Mulek, Jacob tries to cut through, but Moroni’s men hold firm.
The fighting is ferocious, with many killed on both sides. Moroni is wounded, and Jacob is killed.
Lehi presses so hard on the rear that the Lamanites there surrender; the rest are confused and don’t know where to go or whom to fight.
Seeing their confusion, Moroni offers mercy: give up your weapons, and we will stop shedding your blood.

f.g: Refrain; hold back.

chapters.n: The surviving chief captains throw their weapons at Moroni’s feet and order their men to do likewise.
Many refuse; they are bound, disarmed, and marched with the others to Bountiful.
Remarkably, more prisoners are taken than the total killed on both sides—a reflection of Moroni’s preference for capture over slaughter.
Under guard, the Lamanite prisoners are made to bury both their own dead and the Nephite dead.
Moroni gives command of Mulek to Lehi, his companion in most of his battles. The two were alike in character, loved each other, and were loved by all the Nephites.
Once the burials are done, the prisoners return to Bountiful, where Teancum, by Moroni’s orders, puts them to work digging a ditch around the city.
They build a timber breastwork on the inner bank of the ditch and pile dirt against it, until Bountiful is ringed with a very high wall of timber and earth.

f.g: A chest-high defensive wall.

chapters.n: Bountiful becomes a lasting stronghold, and the prisoners are held inside the very wall they built. Keeping them at work made them easy to guard and freed Moroni’s troops for battle.
Moroni has defeated one of the largest Lamanite armies, taken one of their strongest cities, and built a secure prison for captives.
For the rest of the year, Moroni fights no more battles. He fortifies, protects women and children from famine, and gathers food for the armies.

f.g: Severe shortage of food.

chapters.n: Meanwhile, on the southwestern front, the Lamanites gain ground and take several cities while Moroni is distracted by “intrigue”—secret plotting—among the Nephites.

f.g: Secret scheming or plotting.

chapters.n: Mormon repeats a key lesson: internal sin, dissension, and plotting put the Nephites in their greatest danger.
Mormon turns to the people of Ammon—Lamanites converted by the word of God through Ammon and his brothers, who had moved to Nephite lands and been protected ever since.
They had sworn never to shed blood again and would have let themselves be killed rather than break that oath, if not for the love Ammon and his brothers showed them.

f.w: they never would shed blood more

chapters.n: That love is why they were brought to Zarahemla and protected by the Nephites.
Seeing how much the Nephites were suffering on their behalf, they felt compassion and wanted to take up arms to help defend the country.
Helaman and his brethren persuade them not to, because they were about to break their sacred oath.
Helaman feared that breaking their covenant could cost them their souls. So these men had to watch their protectors suffer, unable to help in the usual way.
But they had many sons who had never made that covenant. Those old enough to fight gathered and called themselves Nephites.
These young men covenant to fight for Nephite liberty, to defend the land with their lives, and never to give up their freedom.
Two thousand young men make this covenant and take up arms.
The people of Ammon had always been a blessing to the Nephites, and now these sons become a great support. They ask Helaman to be their leader.
These young men are brave, strong, and active—and above all, true at all times in whatever they are entrusted with.
They are men of truth and seriousness, raised to keep God’s commandments and walk uprightly. Their character came from their parents’ teaching.

f.g: Seriousness and self-control.

chapters.n: Helaman marches at the head of his two thousand “stripling” soldiers to help defend the southwestern borders by the west sea.

f.g: A young man, a youth.

chapters.n: So ends the twenty-eighth year of the judges (about 64 BC).
At the start of the twenty-ninth year (about 63 BC), King Ammoron writes to Moroni proposing an exchange of prisoners.
Moroni is delighted. Freeing Lamanite prisoners would save food for his own people, and getting Nephite captives back would strengthen his army.

f.g: Supplies of food.

chapters.n: But the Lamanites hold many Nephite women and children, while Moroni holds only soldiers. So he plans a strategy to recover as many Nephite captives as possible.

f.g: A clever plan.

chapters.n: Moroni writes a letter and sends it back with Ammoron’s messenger. Here is his letter.

f.g: A letter.

chapters.n: Moroni addresses Ammoron directly about the war begun by his brother and continued by him.
He warns that God’s justice and the sword of His wrath hang over Ammoron unless he repents and withdraws to the land of Nephi.

f.w: the sword of his almighty wrath

chapters.n: Moroni would gladly explain the hell awaiting murderers like Ammoron and his brother—if Ammoron were capable of listening.
Since Ammoron has already rejected these truths and fought the Lord’s people, Moroni expects him to do so again.
The Nephites are ready. If Ammoron doesn’t change course, he will bring God’s wrath on himself to his complete destruction.
As surely as the Lord lives, Nephite armies will attack unless he withdraws. They will keep their cities, lands, religion, and God’s cause.

f.g: A solemn oath: “as surely as God lives.”

chapters.n: Suspecting his warnings are wasted on a “child of hell,” Moroni sets hard terms: one Lamanite prisoner for one Nephite man plus his wife and children.

f.g: It seems to me; I suppose.

chapters.n: If refused, Moroni will arm even women and children, pursue the Lamanites into the land of Nephi—the Nephites’ first inheritance—and fight “blood for blood” until they are destroyed.

f.w: the land of our first inheritance

chapters.n: Moroni admits he writes in anger. The Lamanites tried to murder them; the Nephites only defended themselves. Further attacks will bring a counterattack to reclaim their homeland.
He signs simply: “I am Moroni; I am a leader of the people of the Nephites.”
Ammoron is angered by the letter and writes his own reply.
He introduces himself as king of the Lamanites and brother of Amalickiah, whom he says Moroni murdered, and vows revenge without fear.
He repeats the old Lamanite grievance: the Nephites’ ancestors stole the right to rule from their older brothers.

f.w: rob them of their right to the government

chapters.n: If the Nephites surrender and submit to the “rightful” rulers, Ammoron says, the war will end.
He brushes off Moroni’s threats, repeating that he is not afraid—bold words from a king whose brother died in his own tent.
Still, he gladly agrees to exchange prisoners to save food for his soldiers, but promises an endless war until the Nephites are conquered or wiped out.
He scoffs at God: he doesn’t know such a being, and says Moroni doesn’t either. If God exists, perhaps He made the Lamanites too.

f.w: we know not such a being

chapters.n: He sneers that if there is a devil and hell, Moroni will end up there with Amalickiah—then dismisses the whole subject.
A revealing detail: Ammoron is a descendant of Zoram, Laban’s servant whom Nephi brought out of Jerusalem. He is a Nephite dissenter, not a Lamanite by descent.

f.g: Forced or compelled.

chapters.n: Yet he calls himself “a bold Lamanite,” fighting to avenge Lamanite wrongs and claim their right to govern. With that, he ends his letter.
Ammoron’s letter angers Moroni even more. He knows Ammoron, a Zoramite, fully understands that his war is built on fraud, not a just cause.

f.g: Deception; here, the false pretext for the war.

chapters.n: Moroni refuses to exchange prisoners unless Ammoron gives up his aims. He won’t hand the enemy any more strength than it already has.
Moroni knows where the Nephite captives are held. Since Ammoron rejected his terms, he will act on his words and fight until the Lamanites beg for peace.

f.g: Formally ask for peace.

chapters.n: Moroni has his army searched for a descendant of Laman.
They find a man named Laman, a former servant of the Lamanite king murdered by Amalickiah—one of those who fled to the people of Ammon.

f.w: the king who was murdered by Amalickiah

chapters.n: Moroni sends Laman and a few men toward the guards over the Nephite prisoners.
The prisoners are held in the city of Gid.
At evening Laman approaches the guards, assures them he is a Lamanite who escaped from the sleeping Nephites, and says he brought some of their wine.

f.g: Called out to; challenged.

chapters.n: The tired guards welcome him and ask for the wine.
Laman suggests saving the wine for battle—a bit of reverse psychology that only makes them want it more.
They argue they’re weary now and will get more wine as rations later to strengthen them for battle.

f.g: Fixed portions of food or drink given to soldiers.

chapters.n: Laman lets them do as they wish.
They drink freely. The wine tastes good and was prepared to be especially strong, so they drink even more.
They grow merry and eventually all become drunk.
When the guards are drunk and asleep, Laman and his men report back to Moroni.
This was Moroni’s plan. He goes to Gid with armed men and silently tosses weapons over the wall to the prisoners until all are armed.
Even women and children able to handle a weapon are armed—all done in complete silence.

f.g: Absolute quiet.

chapters.n: Had they woken the Lamanites, the drunk guards would have been easy to kill.
But Moroni didn’t want that. He took no pleasure in killing, only in saving his people. To avoid injustice, he would not slaughter men who were helplessly drunk.

f.w: he did not delight in murder or bloodshed

chapters.n: He achieved his goal: the prisoners inside the walls were armed and able to take control of the inner city.
Moroni pulls his men back a short distance and surrounds the Lamanite army.

f.g: A short distance.

chapters.n: All this happens at night. At dawn the Lamanites wake to find Nephites surrounding them outside and armed prisoners inside.
Seeing they are trapped, the Lamanite captains throw their weapons at the Nephites’ feet and plead for mercy.
Exactly as Moroni hoped: he takes the Lamanites prisoner, captures the city, and frees all the Nephite captives, who join and greatly strengthen his army.
Moroni puts the Lamanite prisoners to work strengthening Gid’s fortifications.
Once Gid is fortified, the prisoners are moved to Bountiful, which is guarded by a strong force.
Despite Lamanite schemes, the Nephites keep their prisoners and hold all the ground they have retaken.

f.g: Secret plots.

chapters.n: The Nephites begin winning again and reclaiming their rights and privileges.
The Lamanites try many night attacks to surround them but lose many men as prisoners in the attempts.
They also repeatedly try to get the Nephites to drink poisoned or intoxicating wine—turning Moroni’s own trick against him.
The Nephites remember the Lord in their trials and avoid the trap. They won’t drink any wine without first giving some to Lamanite prisoners.

f.g: Traps.

chapters.n: Their reasoning was simple: wine that would poison a Lamanite would poison a Nephite. So they tested all their drinks.

f.g: Alcoholic drinks or other liquids.

chapters.n: Moroni now prepares to attack Morianton, which the Lamanites have turned into a powerful stronghold.
The Lamanites keep sending new troops and supplies into Morianton.
So ends the twenty-ninth year of the judges (about 63 BC).
On the second day of the thirtieth year (about 62 BC), Moroni receives a letter from Helaman describing the war on the southwestern front. Chapters 56–58 contain this letter.
Helaman greets Moroni warmly as a beloved brother, both in the gospel and in the hardships of war.

f.g: Severe trials and suffering.

chapters.n: He reminds Moroni that his soldiers are sons of the converts Ammon brought from the land of Nephi—descendants of Laman, Lehi’s eldest son.
He doesn’t need to recount their ancestors’ traditions and unbelief, since Moroni knows them.

f.g: Repeat or recount.

chapters.n: It is enough to say that two thousand of these young men took up arms, asked Helaman to lead them, and came out to defend their country.
Moroni also knows their fathers’ covenant never to take up arms against their brethren.

f.w: the covenant which their fathers made

chapters.n: In the twenty-sixth year, seeing Nephite suffering on their behalf, the fathers were ready to break that covenant to help.
Helaman wouldn’t let them, trusting God would strengthen the Nephites so that no one would suffer more because of the fathers keeping their oath.
Now the good news: in the twenty-sixth year Helaman led the two thousand to the city of Judea to help Antipus, the commander Moroni had appointed there.

f.g: A Nephite commander; not the mountain Antipas in Lamanite territory.

chapters.n: Helaman calls them his “two thousand sons,” and says they deserve the title. Antipus rejoices at the reinforcements, since his army had suffered heavy losses.
They take comfort that the fallen died for their country and their God, and are happy.
The Lamanites took many prisoners, but only chief captains; they spared no one else. Helaman assumes these captains are in the land of Nephi, if still alive.
Helaman lists the cities the Lamanites captured at the cost of many brave Nephite lives.
They are Manti, Zeezrom, Cumeni, and Antiparah.
When Helaman arrived at Judea, Antipus’s men were straining to fortify the city.
They were worn out in body and spirit after fighting by day and laboring by night.

f.g: Weighed down; exhausted.

chapters.n: Resolved to win or die there, they were greatly encouraged by Helaman’s small band of young soldiers.
Seeing Antipus reinforced, the Lamanites were ordered by Ammoron not to attack Judea.
Helaman sees God’s hand here: had the Lamanites attacked during that weak moment, they might have destroyed the small army.
Ammoron ordered his forces to hold the captured cities. The twenty-sixth year ended, and by the twenty-seventh the Nephites had fortified Judea.
The Nephites wanted the Lamanites to attack them rather than attack well-fortified cities themselves.
They posted spies to make sure the Lamanites couldn’t slip past by day or night to attack weaker cities to the north.
Those northern cities were too weak to resist alone. The plan was to hit any passing Lamanite army from behind while others met it in front—but the Lamanites didn’t cooperate.
The Lamanites didn’t dare pass with their whole army or with part of it, fearing defeat.

f.g: Dared.

chapters.n: Nor did they dare march on Zarahemla or cross the head of the Sidon to Nephihah.
So the Lamanites stayed put, determined to hold the cities they had taken.
In the second month, the fathers of the two thousand sent many provisions—the covenant-keeping parents supporting the war in the way they could.

f.w: the fathers of those my two thousand sons

chapters.n: Two thousand more men arrived from Zarahemla, bringing the force to ten thousand, with food for them and their families.
Seeing the Nephites grow stronger daily, the Lamanites became nervous and began sallying out to cut off supplies.

f.g: Rush out in a sudden attack.

chapters.n: The Nephites plan a trick: Antipus orders Helaman and his “little sons” to march toward a nearby city as if carrying supplies.

f.g: A clever military plan.

chapters.n: They are to pass near Antiparah, seemingly heading for a coastal city beyond.
They set out, appearing to carry provisions.
Antipus follows with part of his army, waiting until Helaman’s force is near Antiparah before moving out.
Antiparah held the strongest and largest Lamanite army.
Warned by spies, that army marches out after Helaman’s men.
Helaman’s force flees north, drawing the most powerful Lamanite army after them.
When the Lamanites see Antipus pursuing behind them, they press straight ahead after Helaman, apparently hoping to destroy his small army before Antipus can catch them.
Seeing the danger, Antipus hurries, but night falls before anyone catches anyone, and all camp.
Before dawn the Lamanites resume the chase. Too weak to fight, and unwilling to let his young men be captured, Helaman leads them into the wilderness.
Neither side dares turn aside, so they flee all day into the wilderness until dark.
The next morning the Lamanites are upon them again, and they keep fleeing.
Then the Lamanites suddenly stop, on the third day of the seventh month.
Helaman doesn’t know whether Antipus has caught them or whether it’s a trap to lure his men back.

f.g: Trap.

chapters.n: So he asks his young soldiers: will you go back and fight?
Helaman tells Moroni he had never seen such courage, not among all the Nephites.
They answer: “Father, our God is with us, and He won’t let us fall.” They don’t want to kill their brethren, but will go so Antipus’s army isn’t overpowered.
Though they had never fought, they didn’t fear death and cared more for their fathers’ liberty than their own lives. Their mothers had taught them that if they did not doubt, God would deliver them.

f.w: they had been taught by their mothers

chapters.n: They repeat their mothers’ words: “We do not doubt our mothers knew it.” Their faith was borrowed at first, then made their own.

f.w: We do not doubt our mothers knew it

chapters.n: Helaman turns back with his two thousand. Antipus has caught up with the Lamanites, and a terrible battle is underway.
Antipus’s army, exhausted from the forced march, is about to be overrun. Without Helaman’s return, the Lamanites would have won.
Antipus and many leaders have fallen, weakened by the hard march. Their leaderless men begin to give way.
The Lamanites chase them eagerly—until Helaman hits their rear with his two thousand, inflicting such losses that the whole Lamanite army turns to face him.
Seeing this, Antipus’s men regroup and strike the Lamanites from behind.
Surrounded by both Nephite forces, the Lamanites surrender their weapons and themselves as prisoners.
After the surrender, Helaman counts his young men, afraid many have died.
To his great joy, not one has fallen. They fought with miraculous strength, as if with God’s own power, frightening the Lamanites into surrendering.

f.w: not one soul of them fallen
as if with the strength of God

chapters.n: With nowhere to hold prisoners safely, Helaman sends them to Zarahemla with some of Antipus’s surviving men, and returns to Judea with the rest and his young Ammonites.

f.g: Young soldiers from the people of Ammon.

chapters.n: Helaman’s letter continues. Ammoron offers to give up Antiparah in exchange for the prisoners Helaman’s forces captured.
Helaman replies that his forces can take Antiparah themselves. Trading prisoners for it would be foolish; he’ll release prisoners only in exchange for Nephite captives.
Ammoron refuses to exchange prisoners, so the Nephites prepare to attack Antiparah.
The Lamanites abandon Antiparah and flee to fortify their other cities, so the city falls to the Nephites without a fight.
So ends the twenty-eighth year of the judges.
Early in the twenty-ninth year, supplies and six thousand reinforcements arrive, along with sixty more young Ammonites, bringing Helaman’s band to two thousand and sixty.

f.w: sixty of the sons of the Ammonites

chapters.n: Now strong and well-supplied, they set their sights on the army guarding the city of Cumeni.
They quickly succeed, surrounding Cumeni by night just before the Lamanites expect a shipment of supplies.
They camp around the city for many nights, sleeping on their swords and posting guards. The Lamanites attack repeatedly at night but are always driven back with losses.

f.g: Sleep with weapons at hand, ready to fight at any moment.

chapters.n: When the supply train finally arrives at night, it finds Nephites instead of Lamanites—and the Nephites capture it.
Cut off, the Lamanites still hold out. The Nephites send the captured supplies to Judea and the prisoners to Zarahemla.
Within days, the Lamanites lose hope of relief and surrender Cumeni.

f.g: Help or relief.

chapters.n: But the prisoners are so many that the Nephites need their entire force to guard them—or else must kill them.
The prisoners break out repeatedly in large groups, fighting with stones and clubs. Over two thousand are killed after surrendering.
The choice is grim: kill them or guard them all the way to Zarahemla. Food is also barely enough for the Nephites themselves.
In this serious dilemma, they choose the merciful option and send the prisoners to Zarahemla under guard.
The next day the guards unexpectedly return—just in time, because Ammoron has sent a large new army and fresh supplies against the Nephites.

f.g: At the right time.

chapters.n: The returning guards arrive in time to stop the Lamanites from overwhelming the Nephites.

f.g: Stop or hold back.

chapters.n: Helaman’s two thousand and sixty fight desperately and hold firm, defeating all who oppose them.
While the rest of the army begins to give way, these young men stand firm and fearless.

f.g: Not discouraged or afraid.

chapters.n: They obey every command exactly, and it is done to them according to their faith. Helaman remembers what their mothers had taught them.
The victory belongs to his young soldiers and the men sent with the prisoners. They drive the Lamanites back to Manti.
The Nephites keep Cumeni and survive, though with heavy losses.
After the battle, Helaman orders the wounded found among the dead and their wounds treated.

f.g: Cleaned and bandaged.

chapters.n: Two hundred of the two thousand and sixty had fainted from blood loss. Yet, to everyone’s astonishment and joy, not one died—though every one had many wounds.

f.w: there was not one soul of them who did perish

chapters.n: While a thousand other Nephites were killed, these young men were spared. Helaman attributes it to God’s miraculous power and their great faith that a just God would preserve those who did not doubt.
Helaman sums up their faith: they are young, but their minds are firm, and they trust God continually.
After caring for the wounded and burying the many dead from both sides, Helaman asks Gid what happened to the prisoners.
Gid was the chief captain assigned to escort the prisoners to Zarahemla.

f.g: A Nephite captain; also the name of a city (Alma 55:7).

chapters.n: Gid reports that on the way, they met Nephite scouts who had been watching the Lamanite camp.
The scouts shouted that the Lamanite armies were marching on Cumeni to destroy the Nephites there.
Hearing this, the prisoners take courage and rebel.
When the guards draw swords, the prisoners rush them in a mass. Most are killed; the rest break through and escape.
Unable to catch them, Gid’s men hurry back to Cumeni and arrive in time to help save the city.
Gid gives God the credit: blessed be His name, for He delivered them and did this great thing.
Helaman is filled with joy at God’s goodness in preserving them, and trusts that the souls of the slain have entered into God’s rest.
Helaman’s next goal is Manti, but the Lamanites remember the earlier decoy tricks and won’t be lured out of their strongholds.

f.g: Lure into a trap.

chapters.n: They far outnumber Helaman’s army, so attacking their fortifications directly is out of the question.

f.g: Dared.

chapters.n: Helaman needs his men to hold the land already regained, so he waits for reinforcements and supplies from Zarahemla.
He sends messengers to the governor to report on their situation and waits for help.

f.g: Pahoran, the chief judge.

chapters.n: But waiting helps little, since the Lamanites are being reinforced and resupplied daily too.
The Lamanites keep raiding, trying to destroy them by cunning, but always retreat to their strongholds before a real battle.

f.g: Making sudden attacks.

chapters.n: For months they wait in hardship until they are near starvation.
Food finally comes, escorted by two thousand men—the only help they receive against a vast enemy.
They don’t know why the government sends so little. Grieved and afraid, they worry that God’s judgments might be falling on the land.

f.g: Difficulties; hindrances.

chapters.n: So they pour out their souls in prayer for strength, deliverance, and the ability to hold their cities and lands.
God answers—not with soldiers or food, but with assurance. He speaks peace to their souls, gives them great faith, and helps them hope for deliverance in Him.

f.w: he did speak peace to our souls

chapters.n: Taking courage, the small force resolves to defeat their enemies and defend lands, families, and liberty.
They march boldly against Manti and camp at the edge of the wilderness near the city.
The next day the Lamanites send spies to gauge the Nephite army’s size and strength.
Seeing the Nephites are few, and fearing their supply lines will be cut, the Lamanites prepare to come out and crush them with superior numbers.
Helaman hides two small groups in the wilderness, one under Gid and one under Teomner.

f.g: Hide.

chapters.n: Gid’s men hide on the right and Teomner’s on the left, while Helaman stays with the main force at their original camp.
When the Lamanite army comes out and is about to attack, Helaman’s men retreat into the wilderness.
The Lamanites chase hard, passing right between Gid’s and Teomner’s hidden forces without spotting them.
Once the army passes, Gid and Teomner emerge and cut off the Lamanite spies so they can’t warn the city.
Then they rush the city, overpower the few guards left behind, and take Manti.
This worked because the Lamanites had let almost their whole army be drawn away, leaving just a few guards.
Gid and Teomner now hold the stronghold. Meanwhile Helaman leads his men through the wilderness toward Zarahemla.
Seeing the Nephites heading for Zarahemla, the Lamanites fear a trap and retreat the way they came.
At nightfall they camp, assuming the Nephites are exhausted and not thinking about Manti, since they believed they had driven off the whole army.
That night Helaman’s men don’t sleep. They march by another route toward Manti.
By morning they have passed the Lamanites and reach Manti first.
By this strategy, they take Manti without shedding any blood.
When the Lamanite army arrives and sees the Nephites ready, they are stunned and terrified and flee into the wilderness.
The Lamanites abandon this entire region, but they take many Nephite women and children with them as captives.
All the captured cities are back in Nephite hands, and families are returning home—except those taken prisoner.
Still, Helaman’s armies are too small to defend so many cities and lands.
But they trust God, who gave them victory and restored their own lands to them.
They still don’t know why the government won’t send more help, and the reinforcements don’t know either.

f.w: the government does not grant us more strength

chapters.n: Helaman graciously allows that perhaps Moroni has had setbacks and needed the forces; if so, they won’t complain.

f.g: Grumble or complain.

chapters.n: Otherwise, he fears some faction in the government is withholding men, since far more are available. (Chapter 61 shows his suspicion was right.)

f.g: A dissenting group within a larger body.

chapters.n: But it doesn’t matter. They trust God to deliver them despite their weakness.
It is late in the twenty-ninth year. The Nephites hold their lands, and the Lamanites have fled to the land of Nephi.
The young sons of Ammon are with Helaman in Manti. The Lord has protected them so that not one has been killed.

f.w: even one soul has not been slain

chapters.n: Though covered with wounds, they stand firm in the liberty God gave them. They remember Him daily, keep His commandments, and have strong faith in prophecies of Christ’s coming.

f.w: that liberty wherewith God has made them free

f.g: God’s laws and decrees.

chapters.n: Helaman closes with a prayer that God, who redeemed them and made them free, will keep Moroni in His presence and help him reclaim all the lost lands. He signs, “Helaman, the son of Alma.”
In the thirtieth year (about 62 BC), Moroni reads Helaman’s letter and rejoices at his remarkable success in reclaiming the lost lands.
He shares the good news with everyone in his region so they can rejoice too.
Moroni immediately writes to Pahoran asking for men to reinforce Helaman so he can hold the lands he so miraculously regained.
Having sent the letter, Moroni begins planning to retake the remaining cities still held by the Lamanites.
While he prepares, the Lamanites attack Nephihah, where refugees from Moroni, Lehi, and Morianton had gathered.
The Lamanite armies driven from Manti and nearby areas have joined forces in this region.
Huge in numbers and growing daily, they attack Nephihah on Ammoron’s orders and slaughter many.
The survivors of Nephihah flee and join Moroni’s army.
Moroni had assumed men would be sent from the government to defend Nephihah. Knowing it is easier to hold a city than retake it, he expected it to stand.
So he had kept all his forces to defend places he had already recovered.
When Nephihah falls, Moroni is grief-stricken. He begins to fear that the people’s wickedness might lead to their defeat by the Lamanites.
His chief captains share this fear, troubled by the people’s wickedness and the Lamanites’ success against them.

f.g: Were astonished.

chapters.n: Moroni becomes angry with the government for its apparent indifference to the country’s freedom—setting up the fiery letter in the next chapter.

f.g: Lack of concern.

chapters.n: Moroni writes again to Pahoran, the chief judge in Zarahemla, and to all the leaders responsible for managing the war.
His letter is a rebuke. He reminds them that their job was to raise, arm, and send soldiers wherever the Lamanites attacked.

f.g: As a formal rebuke or accusation.

chapters.n: He and Helaman’s armies have endured hunger, thirst, exhaustion, and every kind of hardship.
Personal suffering alone wouldn’t make them complain.

f.g: Grumble.

chapters.n: But thousands have died who might have lived if the government had sent enough men and supplies. Their neglect has been great.

f.g: Help; relief.

chapters.n: Moroni demands an explanation for this neglect and “thoughtless state.”
