He asks pointedly: can you sit on your thrones in a careless stupor while enemies murder thousands of your brethren?

f.g: A dazed, inactive state.

chapters.n: These are the people who trusted them and put them in power to protect them—and who could have been saved.
Worse, food was withheld, so soldiers fought and bled to death while nearly starving, all from love for their people.
Moroni calls them “beloved brethren,” but says they should have worked harder. The blood of thousands will be on their heads, for God heard every cry.

f.w: the blood of thousands shall come upon your heads

chapters.n: Did they think God would deliver them while they did nothing? If so, they were mistaken.

f.g: Assumed wrongly.

chapters.n: Nor should they assume the dead were killed for their own wickedness. Many righteous died, and that is to the leaders’ condemnation.
The Lord sometimes allows the righteous to be killed so His justice may fall on the wicked. But the righteous aren’t lost; they enter the Lord’s rest.

f.w: the Lord suffereth the righteous to be slain

chapters.n: Moroni fears God’s judgments will fall on the people because of the government’s laziness and neglect of those who died.

f.g: Laziness.

chapters.n: If not for wickedness beginning at the top, the Nephites could have held off their enemies entirely.

He traces the disaster to the king-men, whose hunger for power sparked civil conflict. If the Nephites had stayed united and gone forth in the Lord’s strength, they would have scattered their enemies.
Instead, Lamanites are seizing land, killing and capturing women and children—all because of power-seekers like the king-men.
Moroni even wonders whether the leaders themselves are seeking power and are traitors to their country.
Or have they ignored the armies simply because they feel safe in the heart of the country?
Have they forgotten God’s commandments, their fathers’ captivity, and all the times God delivered them?
Do they think the Lord will deliver them while they refuse to use the means He has given? Faith requires effort.

f.w: make use of the means which the Lord has provided

chapters.n: Will they sit idle, surrounded by tens of thousands of idle men, while thousands bleed and die on the borders?
God won’t hold them guiltless. Moroni quotes the principle that the inner vessel must be cleansed first, then the outer.

f.w: the inward vessel shall be cleansed first

chapters.n: Unless they repent, get moving, and send food and men to him and Helaman, Moroni will stop fighting the Lamanites and first cleanse the “inner vessel”—the government itself.

f.g: Get busy; take action.

chapters.n: If they don’t respond with a true spirit of freedom, he will leave some of his freemen to hold the land under God’s protection.
He trusts these men because of their great faith and patience in hardship.
Then he will come to Zarahemla and, if even a spark of freedom remains, stir up an uprising until the would-be usurpers are gone.

f.g: Uprisings against authority.
Seize power unlawfully.

chapters.n: Moroni doesn’t fear their power; he fears only God. He defends his country at God’s command, and their iniquity has caused the great losses.
The time is now: unless they rouse themselves to defend the country and their children, the sword of justice hangs over them and will fall.

f.g: Rouse; get moving.

chapters.n: He waits for help. If none comes, he will march to Zarahemla and strike them down so they can no longer obstruct the cause of freedom.

f.g: Hinder or block.

chapters.n: The Lord won’t let them grow strong in sin and destroy His righteous people.
Moroni contrasts motives: Lamanite hatred stems from inherited traditions and dissenters’ agitation, but the leaders’ sins come from love of glory and worldly vanity. Why would God spare them?
They knowingly trample God’s laws. The Lord has told Moroni: if your governors don’t repent, go to battle against them.
Moroni is bound by his covenant to keep God’s commandments, and urges them to follow God’s word and quickly send supplies and men to him and Helaman.

f.g: Compelled; obligated.

chapters.n: If not, he will come quickly. God won’t let his army starve, so He will give them the government’s food—by the sword if necessary.

Moroni’s famous closing: he seeks not power but to pull it down, not worldly honor but God’s glory and his country’s freedom. Chapter 61 reveals Pahoran was innocent, showing how gracious he is in reply.

f.w: I seek not for power, but to pull it down

chapters.n: Moroni had just sent Pahoran a stinging letter accusing the government of neglect. Before long, a reply arrives from Pahoran himself, and Mormon copies it for us in full.
Pahoran opens not with self-defense but with sympathy. Moroni’s suffering hurts him too. His gentle tone, in answer to a harsh letter, sets the mood for the whole reply.

f.g: Another name for the chief judge, the highest civil office among the Nephites in this era.

chapters.n: The real reason help never came: a rebellion at home. Some people are actually glad to see Moroni struggling, and they have risen against Pahoran and the loyal freemen in large numbers.

f.g: Nephites who supported free government by judges, as opposed to the “king-men.”

chapters.n: The rebels want the judgment-seat for themselves. Using flattery, they won many followers, cut off supplies to the army, and frightened loyal men from joining Moroni. This explains the neglect Moroni complained about.

f.g: Discouraged or intimidated.

chapters.n: Pahoran himself has been forced out of the capital, Zarahemla, and has taken refuge in the land of Gideon with whatever men he could gather.

f.g: A Nephite land east of the river Sidon, named after the faithful Gideon.

chapters.n: From Gideon, Pahoran sent out a call for help, and loyal citizens are arriving every day, ready to fight for their country, their freedom, and to set right the wrongs done to them.

f.g: A public announcement or call to arms.

chapters.n: The growing loyalist force is now strong enough that the rebels are afraid to attack it. The situation is a stand-off rather than a defeat.

f.g: Dared not.

chapters.n: The rebels hold Zarahemla, have crowned a king, and made a secret deal with the Lamanite king: hold the capital so the Lamanites can conquer the rest, then rule as a puppet king. It is outright treason.
Here is the heart of the letter. Pahoran is not offended by Moroni’s accusations; he admires Moroni’s zeal. He wants office only to protect his people’s liberty, a freedom he sees as God-given.

f.g: Sharply criticized or blamed.

f.w: liberty in the which God hath made us free

chapters.n: Pahoran explains when force is justified. They will resist evil even to the point of bloodshed, yet they have no wish to harm the Lamanites if the Lamanites would simply stay home.
The same principle applies to fellow Nephites: the freemen would never fight their own brothers unless those brothers first took up arms in rebellion.
Pahoran is willing even to accept bondage if God’s justice required it or God commanded it. His loyalty is to God first, not to winning.

f.g: A metaphor from oxen harnessed together: being put under someone else’s control.

chapters.n: But God has not asked them to surrender. He has asked them to trust Him, with the promise that He will deliver them. Faith, not passivity, is the command.
Pahoran’s rule of thumb: answer evil with words where words work; where they fail, as in armed rebellion, use the sword. The goal is freedom, including freedom to worship and serve the Redeemer.
He asks Moroni to come quickly with a small force, leaving his trusted captains Lehi and Teancum to run the war in the east, guided by the Spirit of God, which Pahoran calls the spirit of freedom.
Pahoran has managed to send a few supplies to Lehi and Teancum so their armies will not starve while Moroni is away.
Moroni should recruit along the way, and together they will move against the rebels, relying on God’s strength and their own faith.

f.g: Those who broke away from the Nephite government and its laws.

chapters.n: Retaking Zarahemla matters doubly: it ends the rebellion and frees the capital’s food supplies for the starving armies at the front.

f.w: in the strength of the Lord

chapters.n: Pahoran confesses he had been unsure whether it was right to fight his own countrymen. Moroni’s letter, far from offending him, helped settle the question.
Moroni had written that the Lord commanded him to go against the rebels if they would not repent. That revelation gave Pahoran the moral clarity he had been looking for.
Pahoran closes warmly, calling Moroni his beloved brother. He asks him to encourage Lehi and Teancum not to fear, because God delivers all who hold fast to God-given liberty.
Moroni’s relief is huge. The man he had suspected of betrayal turns out to be a loyal ally. His joy shows how much the cause of freedom, not his own pride, mattered to him.
Mixed with his joy is grief. Those who drove Pahoran out had turned against both their country and their God, and Moroni mourns that betrayal.

f.g: In short; to sum up.

chapters.n: Following Pahoran’s plan exactly, Moroni takes a small force toward Gideon and leaves Lehi and Teancum in command of the main army.

f.w: according to the desire of Pahoran

chapters.n: Along the way Moroni raises the “standard of liberty,” the banner he once made from his torn coat, inviting everyone who loved freedom to join him.

f.g: Moroni’s “title of liberty,” a banner calling people to defend God, religion, freedom, peace, and families.

chapters.n: The response is overwhelming. Thousands rally to the banner and take up swords so they will not fall into bondage.
United with Pahoran’s men, Moroni’s army now outnumbers the forces of Pachus, the rebel “king” who had seized Zarahemla from the freemen.

f.g: The king-men’s leader in Zarahemla, mentioned only here; he had allied himself with the Lamanites.

chapters.n: Moroni and Pahoran march on the capital and meet the rebel army in battle.
The rebellion collapses. Pachus is killed, his men are captured, and Pahoran takes back the judgment-seat as the lawful chief judge.
The captured rebels and imprisoned king-men are tried under the law. Those who fought against their country in wartime were executed. Mormon stresses that this was done by legal process, not revenge.
In a time of invasion, treason threatened everyone’s survival, so the law was enforced strictly. Mormon presents this as an emergency measure for the nation’s safety.

f.g: Necessary or fitting for the situation.

chapters.n: So ends the thirtieth year of the judges (around 62 BC). Order is restored in Zarahemla, and the internal threat to freedom has been removed.
With the capital secure, Moroni immediately sends food and 6,000 soldiers to Helaman, whose stripling warriors and armies had been starving in the west.
An equal force of 6,000 men with food goes to Lehi and Teancum in the east. The whole Nephite line is finally being supplied.
Leaving a garrison in Zarahemla, Moroni and Pahoran march toward Nephihah, a city the Lamanites had captured, determined to win it back.
On the way they defeat a large Lamanite force, killing many and seizing their supplies and weapons.
Rather than slaughter or imprison the survivors, they have them promise never again to fight the Nephites. Covenants like this were taken very seriously in this culture.
About 4,000 former enemy soldiers are sent to live among the people of Ammon, the converted Lamanites. It is an act of mercy that turns enemies into neighbors.

f.g: Also called the Anti-Nephi-Lehies; Lamanite converts who buried their weapons.

chapters.n: The army continues on and camps on the open plains just outside the city of Nephihah.
Moroni hoped to fight in the open, but the Lamanites, intimidated by his army’s courage and size, stay behind the city walls.

f.g: Dared not.

chapters.n: That night Moroni personally climbs to the top of the wall to scout where the enemy army is sleeping. Like other great captains in this book, he leads from the front.
The Lamanites are camped by the east entrance, all asleep. Moroni has his men prepare strong ropes and ladders to climb down inside the walls.
The army climbs the wall on the west side, far from the sleeping enemy, and lowers itself into the city.
By dawn the entire Nephite army is quietly inside the walls. A night of careful work replaces a costly assault.
Waking to find their enemies already inside, the Lamanites panic and flee through the pass out of the city.
Moroni pursues, killing many and capturing others. The rest escape to the land of Moroni on the eastern seacoast.

f.g: A Nephite land on the east sea, named after Captain Moroni.

chapters.n: Nephihah is retaken without a single Nephite death. Mormon repeatedly highlights moments like this, when careful planning and God’s help spare lives.

f.w: without the loss of one soul

chapters.n: Many Lamanite prisoners now want to join the people of Ammon and live as free people. The gospel community had become attractive even to enemies.
Their wish is granted. Choice, not force, governs who joins.
All the prisoners join the people of Ammon and become productive farmers and herders. This also frees the Nephites from the heavy cost of guarding and feeding prisoners.

f.g: Plowing and farming the land.

chapters.n: Having shrunk the Lamanite army and freed many Nephite captives, Moroni grows stronger and moves on toward the land of Lehi.
Once again the Lamanites retreat as soon as they see Moroni coming.
Moroni chases them from city to city until his army meets Lehi and Teancum’s forces. Caught between them, the Lamanites flee down the coast to the land of Moroni.
The whole Lamanite army is now gathered in one place, and Ammoron, their king, is with them.

f.g: Brother of Amalickiah; a Nephite dissenter who became Lamanite king after Amalickiah’s death.

chapters.n: The Nephite captains surround the Lamanites, trapping them against the wilderness to the south and east.
Both armies are exhausted and no one plans a night attack, except Teancum. He blames Ammoron and his brother Amalickiah for years of war, bloodshed, and famine, and he burns with anger against them.

f.g: A clever plan or trick in war.

chapters.n: Teancum slips into the enemy camp alone, finds the king, and spears him near the heart, just as he had once killed Amalickiah in his tent. But Ammoron wakes his servants before dying, and they catch and kill Teancum.

f.g: A light spear for throwing.

chapters.n: Moroni and Lehi deeply grieve Teancum, a brave, loyal friend of liberty who had suffered much. “The way of all the earth” is a gentle phrase for death.

f.w: gone the way of all the earth
f.g: An old Hebrew idiom for dying.

chapters.n: The next day Moroni attacks, defeats the Lamanites decisively, and drives them out of Nephite lands. They do not come back for some time.
So ends the thirty-first year of the judges. Mormon pauses to sum up: many years of war, bloodshed, famine, and suffering.
The Nephites themselves were far from perfect, with murder, strife, and wickedness among them. Yet they were preserved because of the righteous and especially their prayers.
A key insight: the same long trial affected people in opposite ways. Some grew hard and bitter; others became humble and drew near to God. Hardship does not decide who we become; our response does.
After fortifying the exposed borders, Moroni returns to Zarahemla. Helaman goes home, and peace finally settles over the land.
Moroni hands command to his son Moronihah and retires to live out his days in peace. His heroic career ends quietly, not with power-seeking.
Pahoran resumes governing, and Helaman returns to preaching. War had left the church disordered, so it needed to be set in order again.

f.g: A setting in order; reorganizing the church.

chapters.n: Helaman and his fellow preachers teach with power. Many recognize their sins, repent, and are baptized.
The church is rebuilt throughout the whole land.
Civil life is restored too: laws are reorganized and judges, including chief judges, are chosen by the people.
Peace brings prosperity. The Nephites grow in numbers, strength, and great wealth.

f.g: To grow or become.

chapters.n: Remarkably, this time wealth does not make them proud. They stay humble and remember God. Mormon notes this because it so rarely happens in the “pride cycle.”
Their humility is rooted in memory. They remember how the Lord rescued them from death, captivity, and enemies.
They pray constantly, and the Lord blesses them as He promised: keep the commandments and prosper in the land.
The book of Alma’s war chapters close with the death of Helaman, Alma’s son, in the thirty-fifth year of the judges (about 57 BC).
With Helaman gone, his brother Shiblon becomes keeper of the sacred records and relics that Alma had entrusted to Helaman, about 56 BC.

f.g: The plates, the interpreters, and other sacred objects kept by the Nephite record keepers.

chapters.n: Mormon describes Shiblon as just and upright, someone who kept trying to do good. Mormon adds that his brother was the same, likely meaning Corianton, who had repented after Alma’s counsel.
Captain Moroni dies as well, only a few years after retiring. The great defender of liberty passes quietly, without ceremony in the record.
A major migration begins: 5,400 men, plus their wives and children, leave Zarahemla for the land northward. Many families were looking for new land after the long war.
Hagoth, a man full of curiosity and adventure, builds a very large ship near the narrow neck of land and launches it into the western sea.

f.g: Here, likely skillful and inventive, as well as eager to explore.

chapters.n: Many Nephites, including women and children, board with plenty of supplies and sail northward along the coast.
The next year Hagoth builds more ships. The first one returns, takes on more passengers and supplies, and sets out again.

Some ships were never heard from again. Mormon honestly admits what he does not know, guessing they were lost at sea. Many Latter-day Saints have long believed some of these voyagers reached the Pacific islands.

f.g: Where; to what place.

chapters.n: The migration northward continues by land and sea through the thirty-eighth year.
Shiblon dies. Corianton, his brother, has gone north by ship to carry supplies to the settlers, which suggests he had become a trusted servant of the people.
Before dying, Shiblon passes the sacred items to his nephew Helaman, son of the Helaman who led the stripling warriors. The record-keeping line continues in Alma’s family.

Most of the records Helaman kept had been copied and shared widely among the people. Only the parts Alma had ordered withheld, such as the secret plans of the Gadianton-like combinations, were held back.

f.w: commanded by Alma should not go forth

chapters.n: Even so, the original plates were sacred and had to be handed down carefully through each generation. That duty now belongs to the younger Helaman.

f.w: handed down from one generation to another

chapters.n: That same year, Nephite dissenters living among the Lamanites stir them up to anger again. As so often, apostates fuel the conflict.
A large Lamanite army attacks, but Moronihah, Moroni’s son and successor, defeats them and drives them back with heavy losses.
So ends the thirty-ninth year of the judges, about 53 BC.
The book of Alma closes, covering the records kept by Alma, his son Helaman, and Helaman’s brother Shiblon. The next book is named for the younger Helaman.
